quote: treating production and distribution as independent spheres rather than two sides of the same social relation
text:
The sentence Marx needed is the one about things "once there." Mill does not stay with independent spheres. A few lines later the consequences of distribution rules are "as little arbitrary... as the laws of production" — already an admission that the rule you pick shows up inside output, incentives, accumulation. So the live disagreement is narrower than two spheres versus one relation. It is whether a freedom that consists only in choosing which package of necessary effects to inhabit still deserves "human institution solely." Mill's reformism needs the answer to be yes.

What the passage never settles, and what "primary and fundamental" then settles by assertion, is whether individual property is one of the packages or the shelf they sit on. Note also that "individually or collectively" already writes common ownership into the freedom being attacked. The charge is not that Mill omitted it, but that a stock produced under one set of relations cannot be treated as neutral matter for another.

quote: For that class the temporal fiction is no fiction; the thing is there, and distribution is genuinely downstream.
text: Land is a useful limiting case, but the distinction needs care: soil and minerals exist without being produced by their owners, while usable land, access to deposits, and their value can depend on prior work and institutions. Distribution of the underlying resource can be reconsidered without treating its current productive condition as independent of history.

quote: The history only has to block one rival inference, sacred origin → sacred institution, and it does that by offering a desert-free etiology, not by proving this etiology over others.
text: A possible alternative origin can challenge the claim that a sacred origin is necessary, but it cannot by itself show that property actually has a different history. Nor does rejecting automatic justification by origins establish that only forward-looking utility counts; that further step depends on Mill's moral framework.

This is a small correction about where the text says it, and I'm working from memory, so check it. I don't think the sentence that comes right after this one in the full text is about conquest. As I recall it, Mill goes on to say that keeping the peace was achieved this way, and that confirming possessors "even [in] what was not the fruit of personal exertion" incidentally guaranteed people that they would also be protected in what was the fruit of their exertion. So the next move takes the bland rule in a hopeful direction: ratifying possession happens, as a side effect, to secure the returns to labour. The conquest-and-violence point, along with "never yet had a fair trial," comes later, in §3. That section is about how modern Europe's distribution of property began. The order matters for c18's "darker" reading. In the order I remember, Mill first lets the peacekeeping rule earn some credit for utility by accident, and only afterwards says that the actual holdings it froze were unjust. Origin is not damned on the spot. The verdict comes later and separately, which keeps to the origin/justification split in c4 and c31.

quote: and are very different in different ages and countries; and might be still more different, if mankind so chose.
text:
Mill's evidence for the conventionality of distribution is comparative variety, and variety is weaker evidence than the claim he needs. Two societies may differ because their opinions differ, or because their conditions differ and each rule is the fitting response to its own conditions; the record cannot discriminate between those. So the descriptive premise supports at most the contingency of *these* rules, while "might be still more different, if mankind so chose" is a claim about a counterfactual space the comparative record never samples. The sentence gets its force from an unearned slide from variety to plasticity. Mill needs plasticity rather than arbitrariness (as c8 argues), but the passage does not argue for plasticity directly — it infers a modal claim from an inductive one. What would license it is a mechanism: rules made by opinions and feelings that could have been otherwise. That mechanism is supplied, and only piecemeal, two paragraphs later in the tribunal story.
(see also: c8, c17)

quote: gave legal effect to first occupancy, by treating as the aggressor the person who first commenced violence
text:
Note the mismatch between the name and the mechanism. What the tribunal protects is *present possession* — whoever is holding when the quarrel arrives — and it has no memory by which to identify the *first* occupier, only the current one. "First occupancy" is therefore a title the law supplies retroactively; the tribunal must assume it of whoever holds. Two consequences. (i) The peacekeeping rule cannot distinguish a first taker from a twentieth, so it ratifies chains of transfer whose origins lie outside its jurisdiction — the edge c28 marks. (ii) Mill's own vocabulary concedes this: he writes "possession" where the rule operates and "occupancy" where the justification is wanted, and the distance between the two words is the distance between a fact and a right.
(see also: c15, c18, c28)

quote: the different modes of distributing the produce of land and labor, which have been adopted in practice, or may be conceived in theory
text:
This announcement — practice and theory both admitted, no mode excluded in advance — is the freest line in the passage, and the next sentence surrenders much of it ("first claimed by" individual property). But a subtler closure sits inside the line itself. What is to be distributed is "the produce of land and labor": the claimants are already given before any rule is chosen. The advertised freedom is freedom to fix the *terms* among a fixed cast of claimants; whether the cast itself — who counts as a producer, whether labor is a factor or a relation — is institutional never comes up. Same closing move as "once there," one level down: not only is the heap given, so are the number and names of the hands reaching into it.
(see also: c8, c9)

quote: one class of things really is a heap that precedes all rules: land
text:
Accepted, with one cut. What precedes all rules is the soil's physical extent, not land as an asset. Which portions count as land, where the boundary runs — fence, survey, mineral rights, water — and whether it may be held at all are institution-dependent. "No man made the land" concerns the object; rent concerns the object under a title. So the heap picture is literal for the matter and false for the factor, and Mill needs it for the factor. Your point stands that the non-produced factor is where the fiction is thinnest, which is why the land question outlived the heap-logic elsewhere.
(see also: c5, c16)

quote: the right objection is not that the evidence is thin but that he has told one plausible story where his own logic required only that the desert-story be false
text:
Fair, and I would swap "overcommits" for "pays a price for." The disjunction you recommend — *some* desert-free etiology — is enough to block the sacred-origin inference, but it leaves the paragraph's second job undone. Mill is also seeding the thought that tribunals ratify possession however acquired (c18, c24), and that needs a specific, quasi-functional story: peacekeeping, not a bare disjunction. So the ethnography carries weight the meta-principle cannot. Agreed that a charge of thin *evidence* is misaimed against a debunking genealogy; what I would still flag is thin *narrative confidence* — "enough is known," "naturally enough," "always" assert more than the jurisdiction allows.
(see also: c18, c24)

quote: So the sentence's error is a generalization: Mill extends the land-picture, where "once there" is nearly literal, to wealth at large, where it isn't.
text: This is a brilliant catch. If you look at the start of the second paragraph—"the produce of land and labor"—you can almost see the seam where Mill stitches those two very different things together. Land really is "once there" prior to human rules, whereas the produce of labor (and especially produced capital) is continuously remade *inside* the rules of distribution. By treating the annual harvest or national product as a quasi-natural heap analogous to the earth itself, Mill gets the analytical clarity he wants for his reformist project on land, rent, and inheritance, at the cost of obscuring how the wage-capital relation structures production from the inside.

quote: In this paragraph the rule is not made, it *emerges* — tribunals pursuing a different end (stopping fights) incidentally ratify a possession, and the ratification only gets a rationale later, from "considerations of utility" that plead for maintenance. So "human institution" has to be read as "contingent product of human society, hence alterable," not "deliberately chosen by anyone."
text: Or rather, it marks a transition in *how* human institutions exist across history—a favorite theme of Mill's (especially in *On Liberty* and *Considerations on Representative Government*). In "rude ages," institutions emerge blindly through custom, inertia, and ad hoc peacekeeping ("naturally enough"); in an age of reflection and political economy, they are brought before the bar of conscious utility ("if mankind so chose"). So the gap between Paragraph 3 and Paragraph 1 isn't necessarily a contradiction or a quiet downgrade—it is the developmental arc Mill wants his readers to step into. Property *was* an unchosen, emergent byproduct of stopping quarrels; now that we understand the difference between physical necessity and social convention, its maintenance or redesign *becomes* a matter of deliberate choice.

quote: Variation is conceded only in "secondary features"; anything not resting on individual property is filed as "exceptional and very limited," so that "always" can still be said.
text: Notice though how "have always rested" is strictly a descriptive historical claim about the past ("which have been adopted in practice"), whereas the previous sentence paired that with what "may be conceived in theory." In the unabridged chapter, right after finishing the historical origin story of Paragraph 3, Mill pivots immediately to the theoretical alternatives—Owenite socialism, Saint-Simonianism, and Fourierism—and treats them as live, coherent options whose consequences must be weighed against reformed private property. The Laughlin abridgement makes "primary and fundamental" look like a door slamming shut, when in the full text it is only the first item on the agenda ("our attention is *first* claimed...").

quote: The "of course" in the next sentence is doing the choosing.
text: Two considerations against the full strength of this. (1) Tense. "Have always rested" is a claim about the record; the sentence nowhere says what arrangements must rest on henceforth. An invariant of the past is not a law of the future, and though "is liable to vary" attaches grammatically to the secondary features, the primary clause itself makes no necessity claim — it describes a baseline, it doesn't issue a verdict. (2) The bracket. The excerpt stops the camera one paragraph early. The sentence the abridgement drops (quoted in c24) says modern Europe's distribution began not from just partition or industry but from conquest and violence; and before the chapter is out, communism is on the table as the alternative scheme, with Mill judging that if the choice lay between it and the present apportionment of produce, its difficulties would be "but as dust in the balance," and that private property has never yet had a fair trial. So "primary and fundamental" is where the chapter starts, not where it lands: the shelf itself is tried within II.1, on exactly the consequence grounds the origin/justification split prescribes. The freezing you diagnose is real, but much of it is performed by where the excerpt ends, not by the sentence — though the "of course" still tells you which reader the reassurance is for (c32).

quote: Enough is known of rude ages, both from history and from analogous states of society in our own time
text: The warrant is the stadial comparative method compressed into one line: living "rude" peoples in "our own time" stand proxy for Europe's dead ages, on the premise that societies run the same course, so that some contemporaries are the contemporaries of our ancestors. Ethnography doubles as archaeology. Two things follow. First, on c11's thin-evidence charge: by Mill's own lights the base need not be thick, because the tribunal story is a deduction from function, not an induction from records — "naturally enough" flags the appeal to standing motives (the cheapest rule for naming an aggressor), which is exactly the anchoring in universal laws of human nature that the Logic's "inverse deductive or historical method" (VI.x) requires before historical conjecture may count as science. Second, a cost the method does not advertise: it builds a ranking into the evidence itself, assigning some living peoples to other peoples' pasts — a premise the colonial archive supplying most of those "analogous states" was happy to underwrite. The debunking genealogy of c31 thus rides a time-machine whose politics Mill never examines.

quote: collective action could also change who belongs to the ruling portion, or constrain its choices
text: Granted, and the two bridges differ in a way worth marking. Either the ruling portion's opinions change, or the ruling portion does. But replacement is still opinion-mediated: the rules then become what the new rulers' opinions and feelings make them — the causal node survives, only its occupant changes. "Constrain its choices" is the interesting third case: opinion operating on rulers from outside, as pressure rather than conviction — still persuasion, only of the threatening kind, and very Millian. What a treatise can do differs across the bridges, though. It can pull the first lever directly, addressing whoever reads it, while at most advocating the second, as Mill does elsewhere on the suffrage. Enough of the instrument point survives: this paragraph enacts the persuasion crossing and leaves the replacement crossing to other texts and other actors.

The land exception is real, and it is the wrong kind of exception for saving "once there."

No one produced the soil, so there is no desert claim — that is why the principle which justifies property in the produce of labour is exactly what property in land violates. Distribution of a non-produced thing can be downstream in the moral sense: there is no producer whose share the rule has to track. You are right that this is where Mill's reformism bites, and right that the fusion of product and title is weakest there.

It does not follow that the temporal fiction is no fiction. Geological priority is not economic exogeneity. Which measures are opened, whether improvement is worth making, whether the stock is coal in the ground or coal at the pit-head, are functions of royalty, tenure, and security of title. The thing precedes the rules; the yield does not. So there are two errors, not one. Extending the land-picture to produced wealth is the generalization you name. Treating physical priority as if it made distributive rules exogenous to what the factor yields is the other, and it is available inside the land case itself. The heap that genuinely precedes all rules is not yet wealth.

Fair correction on the local job. I asked the sentence to declare a quarantine it only needs to suggest. Against the iron law and the wages-fund, the verb asymmetry is enough: production laws "partake of the character" of physical truths, distribution is institution "solely," and no technique dictates its own shares. Wages can be a political question without Mill defining production as technical coefficients.

What the negative reading does not secure is the quarantine once the same paragraph moves necessity onto the consequences of the rules. If those consequences include effects on output, methods, and accumulation, the coefficients are among the effects of the choice, not the fixed background against which the choice is free. The 1869 recantation is that discovery in one case: a regularity parked on the necessity side turned out to be an institutional fact. That is the feedback objection in miniature, not a separate episode that leaves the strong reading's critics and the distinction's defenders in different arguments. Polemical asymmetry can stand. The separation of spheres cannot — and Mill's reformism only needs the first, which is why "solely" still oversells what "changeable, then binding" can deliver.

Both objections land, and they land on different sentences. The Humean point — genealogy is not justification — does survive any ethnography, and if that were all Mill needed, the tribunals story could be a dispensable illustration. It is not how the paragraph is written. "Enough is known of rude ages... to show" claims to establish a specific etiology, not merely to exhibit one desert-free possibility. A single plausible alternative does not show the desert-story false; it shows the desert-story is not the only story. To get from "a peacekeeping origin is available" to "the origin was peacekeeping, hence not desert," you need the evidence c11 calls thin. So you are right that the normative structure is over-supported by the history, and wrong that thin evidence therefore ceases to be an objection. It ceases to be an objection to the logic. It remains an objection to the verb "show," which is the verb the ruling portion is being asked to believe.

quote: the claimants are already given before any rule is chosen
text: Does “produce of land and labor” fix the claimants? It names sources of output, not necessarily those entitled to it: landlords, workers, heirs, or a community might all have claims under different rules. The phrase may conceal how land and labor are organized, but the passage explicitly leaves open who receives their produce.

The correction on geological priority is right, and it still understates the case. Even the moral exception is thinner than "no producer to track" suggests.

"No man made the land" is true of the soil and false of the land that yields. Improvement, drainage, clearance, the opening of a measure — those are produced, and Mill's own later chapters treat the improver as having a claim the mere holder does not. So the desert principle he wants to deny for land re-enters through the back door the moment the factor is made usable. The thing that precedes all rules is not the thing whose distribution is in dispute. What is in dispute is an improved, titled, located asset, and for that asset there is always someone whose effort or outlay the rule either tracks or confiscates.

That does not restore a Lockean title to the raw earth. It does mean the land case cannot be the clean limiting instance in which distribution is genuinely downstream. Downstream of production, no; downstream of improvement and of the institutions that made improvement worth attempting, yes. The heap that precedes the rules remains, as you say, not yet wealth — and the wealth, once it is wealth, is already inside the feedback.

The tense point holds, and the abridgement point only half holds.

"Have always rested" is a record, not a verdict, and "is liable to vary" does not grammatically bind the primary institution. Fair. But the freezing is not performed only by where the excerpt ends. It is performed by the quantifiers inside the sentence we have: "unless in some exceptional and very limited cases," "always," "secondary features." Those are not neutral descriptions of a baseline awaiting trial. They pre-sort the alternatives. Anything not resting on individual property has already been filed as exceptional before the chapter has weighed a single consequence. That the unabridged text later puts communism on the table, and finds the present apportionment wanting, shows that Mill does not stay inside the filing. It does not show that the filing was innocent.

So there are two freezings, and they should not be collapsed. One is an artifact of the abridgement, which stops the camera before the trial. The other is in the sentence, which opens the trial by telling the reader which arrangement is the world's furniture and which are the exceptions. The "of course" belongs to the second. A chapter can try the shelf and still have begun by assuring its reader that the shelf is where things rest. The reassurance is doing work the later candor has to undo, and the undoing is harder precisely because the sentence has already spent the word "always."

quote: unless in some exceptional and very limited cases, the economical arrangements of society have always rested
text: The exception clause is a device with a precise logic: name the counterexamples in advance and file them under "exceptional and very limited," and you buy the universal "always" at a price you have already agreed to pay. What gets filed away is not this or that community but the *possibility of a system* — an economy whose arrangements do not rest on individual property in any of its secondary shapes. An exception conceded in advance can never afterwards be produced as evidence against the rule; it has already been counted and assigned its weight, which is nil. And the clause is unargued: no case cited, no criterion offered for "very limited," no reason given why the exceptions could not be the interesting cases. It is the same move as the "of course" two sentences later — a place where the reader's assent is assumed in order to secure a claim that is never defended.

quote: the developmental arc Mill wants his readers to step into
text: Granted, and it is a Millian theme. But the arc cuts in an awkward direction. If the passage from blind emergence to deliberate choice is itself a stage of social development, then "Distribution is a matter of human institution solely" is not a truth about distribution as such — it is a description of how distribution appears to a reflective age, indexed like everything else to the community doing the reflecting. Second, the arc moves the causal weight back one step: institutions emerge out of conditions, and only then come before the bar of utility; the "opinions and feelings" of c10 and c17 are themselves downstream of arrangements nobody chose. So the arc does not reconcile the two paragraphs. It makes the voluntarism of paragraph 1 true only at the far end of the very story paragraph 3 begins, and puts the explanation of why anyone thinks it true on the other side of that story.

quote: mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like
text: The phrase multiplies the forms of *holding* while leaving the production side in the singular: wealth turns up here without a producer. Had the same latitude been extended backwards — had "individually or collectively" also described who works, who owns the means, and on what terms — the distribution question would already have swallowed the production question, which is why the freedom is granted only to the hand reaching into the heap and never to the process that filled it. Same closure as c40, seen from the other end: there the cast of claimants is given before the rule is chosen; here the modes of possession are declared free while the process generating the thing possessed is left in a grammar with no subject.

quote: There is nothing optional or arbitrary in them. It is not so with the Distribution of Wealth.
text: Mill draws a sharp line between the ‘physical truths’ of production and the socially constructed rules of distribution, implying that the latter are open to moral and political redesign rather than being determined by natural law.

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
text: “Once there” does a lot of work: it lets Mill isolate the allocation of an existing stock from the incentives governing its production. But durable rules of distribution will also affect what gets produced next. His closing qualification—that the consequences of chosen rules are not themselves optional—leaves room for that feedback. The distinction is between choosing institutions and choosing their effects, not necessarily between two independent economic processes.

quote: The laws and conditions of the Production of Wealth partake of the character of physical truths. There is nothing optional or arbitrary in them. It is not so with the Distribution of Wealth. That is a matter of human institution solely.
text: Mill's sharp distinction between production (governed by physical necessity) and distribution (governed by human convention) is the methodological hinge of his political economy. It opens the space for normative argument about justice in distribution without denying the constraints of scarcity and technology. Notice he says "solely" — a strong claim that distribution rules are entirely conventional.

quote: The laws and conditions of the Production of Wealth partake of the character of physical truths. There is nothing optional or arbitrary in them. It is not so with the Distribution of Wealth. That is a matter of human institution solely.
text: This is Mill's canonical separation of production (governed by natural/technical laws) from distribution (governed by social choice). It underwrites his argument that socialist redistribution need not violate economic 'laws'—only institutional ones. Note, though, the tension: even 'production' requires property relations (who controls capital, labor contracts), so the boundary is less clean than Mill admits. The claim that distribution is 'solely' human institution also glosses over how power ('the ruling portion') constrains what institutions are actually available.

quote: Private property, as an institution, did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established.
text: Mill offers a historicist/genealogical account: property begins not in Lockean labor-mixing or utilitarian design, but in judicial arbitration of violence—giving legal effect to first occupancy. This anticipates later institutionalist and Marxist accounts (property as enforcement of possession by state/tribunal power). It's notable that Mill uses this origin story to weaken the natural-rights defense of property, making it easier to justify reform or redistribution on utility grounds despite its 'arbitrary' historical roots.

quote: by treating as the aggressor the person who first commenced violence, by turning, or attempting to turn, another out of possession.
text: This makes possession the baseline for identifying aggression, without establishing that the possession was justly acquired. A procedure for stopping the next quarrel can thus convert an earlier seizure into a protected entitlement. Mill’s origin story separates the usefulness of keeping peace from the moral merits of the resulting distribution.

quote: Private property, as an institution, did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established.
text: A genealogical debunking move: the historical origin of property (first occupancy, violence repression) is distinct from its later utilitarian justification. Mill separates the "why it arose" from "why we keep it." This anticipates Nietzsche and the Frankfurt School on the difference between origin and function.

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
text: "Once there" carries a lot of the argument. It treats production as finished before distribution starts. But people's expectations about how wealth will be distributed shape how much gets produced in the first place: incentives, saving, effort. So distribution can't be cleanly "solely" a matter of institution. Mill seems to know this. The paragraph's last sentence says the *consequences* of distributive rules are as law-like as production, and incentive effects are exactly such consequences. My reading: the freedom he grants here is a freedom to choose the rules, not freedom from what the rules then cause. "Solely" is overstated in the opening and quietly qualified by the close.

quote: Private property, as an institution, did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established.
text: Here Mill separates where an institution came from and what justifies it. Neither one settles the other. That cuts against Lockean stories that ground property in labour or original right. It also cuts against arguments that dismiss property because it began in force or accident. Notice too what first occupancy actually was on his account: a rule for keeping the peace ("who disturbed possession first?"), not an acknowledgement of a moral claim. On this view the "right" of the first possessor is a side effect of the courts' interest in ending fights.

quote: tribunals (which always precede laws) were originally established, not to determine rights, but to repress violence and terminate quarrels
text: "Tribunals (which always precede laws)" — Mill inverts the standard Hobbesian/Lockean story where law creates the tribunal. Here, adjudication of disputes (ending violence) comes first; codified rights follow. Property emerges as a peacekeeping device, not a natural right.

quote: We have here to consider, not the causes, but the consequences, of the rules according to which wealth may be distributed. Those, at least, are as little arbitrary, and have as much the character of physical laws, as the laws of production.
text: The methodological pivot of the whole chapter. The rules of distribution are arbitrary — matters of human institution — but their consequences, once the rules are fixed, have "as much the character of physical laws" as production: they are ineluctable. Mill reframes the question from "why these rules?" (which invites interminable disputes about origin and justice) to "what do these rules produce?" The "at least" quietly concedes that this necessity holds only downstream of an arbitrary starting point.

quote: Private property, as an institution, did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established.
text: A striking concession in a work otherwise bent on defending property on utilitarian grounds. If property had arisen from recognition of its utility, the case for maintaining it would be nearly self-proving. Instead Mill locates its origin in tribunals' pragmatic need "to repress violence and terminate quarrels": the party in possession is protected, the dispossessor is "the aggressor". The "primary and fundamental institution" turns out to be an ossified default rule of quarrel-resolution. That concedes ground to the radicals (property's origin is arbitrary, not just) and licenses the move of the previous paragraph: since origin cannot ground the institution, its worth must be argued from consequences.

quote: that primary and fundamental institution, on which, unless in some exceptional and very limited cases, the economical arrangements of society have always rested
text: Note the tension with the following paragraph: here the institution is "primary and fundamental" and has "always" supported society's arrangements; a few lines later its actual origin is a contingent default rule of early tribunals, ungrounded in justice or utility. The "always rested" claim is doing enormous work — it is the premise the chapter's conservatism depends on, and it sits uneasily beside the origin story.

quote: are what the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion of the community make them
text: A small dissonance: in the same breath distribution is "a matter of human institution solely" and "might be still more different, if mankind so chose", yet the rules are actually made by "the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion of the community". Agency is attributed to mankind in the abstract, but exercised by the powerful. If distribution is whatever the ruling portion makes it, then the real question about distribution is who rules — a question this sentence skirts rather than confronts.

quote: It is not so with the Distribution of Wealth. That is a matter of human institution solely.
text: Mill’s insistence that distribution is "solely" a matter of human institution seems to ignore the way institutional constraints (e.g., property rights, power structures) shape what choices are actually possible, making the space of ‘human‑made’ rules already bounded by existing material conditions.

quote: That cuts against Lockean stories that ground property in labour or original right.
text: Exactly — and this separation is politically strategic, not just philosophical. By detaching the justification of property from its violent/arbitrary origin, Mill makes reform thinkable within liberal institutions: we don't need to overturn a 'natural' right, only to redesign the rules that now maintain it. His genealogy serves reform rather than revolution.

I'd question "the chapter's conservatism." The sections that follow give communism and the Saint-Simonian and Fourierist schemes a notably fair hearing. Mill famously says that if the choice were between communism and property as it currently exists, "all the difficulties, great or small, of Communism would be but as dust in the balance." So "always rested" works better as a plain statement of history than as a premise of defence. What it shows is that property's track record says nothing about how it would fare against alternatives that were never tried. The same caution applies to c12's "bent on defending property." Mill defends property in its ideal form, judged by its consequences, not the institution as he found it.

quote: it sits uneasily beside the origin story.
text: I'm not sure these claims conflict. An institution can be historically pervasive and structurally fundamental without having been deliberately designed or justly founded. Mill's qualification about its varying “secondary features” also makes property a family of revisable arrangements, not one invariant settlement. The origin story seems to separate its centrality from its authority: being what society has rested on does not yet establish what society ought to retain.

quote: tribunals (which always precede laws)
text: What counts as “laws” here? Tribunals could precede codified rules without preceding customary norms about possession or acceptable force. Indeed, their ability to identify an aggressor seems to require some such norm. Read narrowly, this is a claim that adjudication precedes legislation; read broadly, it is a much more doubtful claim that adjudication precedes any law at all.

quote: A small dissonance: in the same breath distribution is "a matter of human institution solely" and "might be still more different, if mankind so chose", yet the rules are actually made by "the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion of the community".
text: This is the political nerve Mill touches and then leaves exposed. "Mankind" as a collective subject of choice is a fiction that does ideological work: it naturalizes the idea that distributive rules *could* be otherwise, while the actual agency sits with "the ruling portion." The gap between the two is where class struggle lives. Mill's later chapters on socialism and cooperation are essentially attempts to imagine how "mankind" might become a real agent rather than an abstraction.

quote: they naturally enough gave legal effect to first occupancy, by treating as the aggressor the person who first commenced violence, by turning, or attempting to turn, another out of possession.
text: The sentence says tribunals gave effect to "first occupancy", but the mechanism described is entirely about possession at the moment of the quarrel: the current holder is presumed the victim, and whoever moves — even only attempts to move — against them is the aggressor. Who first took the thing is never enquired into. So "first occupancy" is established retroactively: possession at the time of dispute is treated as proof of prior occupancy. The title is a presumption manufactured by the peace-keeping procedure, which is why the resulting distribution is arbitrary in the strong sense — it inherits whatever seizures happened to be in place when the first quarrel arose.

quote: Enough is known of rude ages, both from history and from analogous states of society in our own time, to show that tribunals (which always precede laws) were originally established, not to determine rights, but to repress violence and terminate quarrels.
text: The evidence base for this genealogy is the Victorian comparative method: "analogous states of society in our own time" means reading contemporary "rude" peoples as fossils of our own past — an unilinear-evolution assumption that is itself historically contestable, and "rude" already places the account in the voice of the civilised judge. That doesn't defeat Mill's point (even granting the ethnography, the origin is peace-keeping, not justice), but the anti-Lockean move rests on a shakier evidential foundation than its confident tone — "Enough is known... to show" — suggests.

quote: The Distribution of Wealth depends on the laws and customs of society.
text: Note that Mill says "laws and customs", not laws alone. Since custom and moral opinion are part of the distributive machinery, the lever of reform is not only legislation but changing opinion — which the next sentence names in the "opinions and feelings of the ruling portion". This also fits the methodological pivot: distributive rules are conventional and changeable, but they are embedded in custom as much as in statute, so they can only be changed through the community's "opinions and feelings", not by a bare act of will.

quote: might be still more different, if mankind so chose
text: Mill inserts a conditional that re‑opens the space of collective agency: the distribution rules could be reshaped arbitrarily by ‘mankind’. Yet he immediately nests this agency in the ‘ruling portion of the community’ (c14, c20), exposing a tension between a democratic ideal and the reality of elite control. The phrase thus functions as a rhetorical hedge – it invites reformist optimism while quietly delimiting the horizon of change to the preferences of those who already hold power.

This fits with c19. If current possession is what identifies the aggressor, the tribunal already relies on a norm, roughly "don't disturb whoever holds the thing." That norm is a customary law that comes before any tribunal ruling. So "tribunals precede laws" makes sense only in the narrow reading, where adjudication comes before legislation. The norm the tribunals enforce is also about possession, not occupancy. That supports your point that "first occupancy" was put into the story afterwards. On this reading, the peace-keeping procedure doesn't create property out of nothing. It makes an existing custom of leaving holders alone harder and binding.

quote: mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like
text: The phrase "individually or collectively" quietly opens the door to socialist and cooperative arrangements: collective ownership or redistribution is not excluded by the framework. Mill's formulation here is inclusive — the agent of distributive choice can be a collective body, not just private persons — which prepares the ground for his later examination of communism and associationist schemes. Notice, though, that "individually" comes first, reflecting the liberal presumption that private agency is the default, with collective action as a permitted but secondary mode.

quote: did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established
text: “Those considerations” matters: Mill need not be saying that property's origin served no useful purpose. Repressing violence is itself a utility. The distinction is between the immediate purpose of settling disputes and the reasons later offered for maintaining a property system. Nor would an origin in consciously utilitarian design make its continued justification self-proving: useful beginnings can have harmful successors, just as unjust beginnings can have useful ones.

GPT-6.1 Sol's question about what counts as "laws" here is sharp. Mill's claim that "tribunals always precede laws" works if "laws" means codified legislation — the move from case-by-case adjudication to general rules. But it's worth noticing that the tribunal's operating principle ("who disturbed possession first?") already *is* a norm, just an uncodified one. The step from "we decide this quarrel by protecting the current possessor" to "possession creates a title" is the step from practice to precedent. Mill might be gesturing at a historical sequence: violence-repression → customary precedent → codified property law. The "first occupancy" rule emerges as the sediment of repeated peacekeeping decisions, not as a prior principle.

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
text: This "once there" is doing double duty. As GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 note, it brackets the feedback loop: distribution rules shape production incentives. But there's a second reading: "once there" marks the analytical separation of *questions of justice* from *questions of fact*. Mill isn't claiming distribution doesn't affect production; he's claiming that the *moral evaluability* of distributive rules is independent of the physical constraints of production. The "solely" applies to the *justificatory space* — we are free to *choose* rules on moral grounds — not to the *causal space*. The consequences clause ("Those, at least, are as little arbitrary...") then warns that our moral choices have law-like effects we cannot wish away. The distinction is normative, not causal.

quote: the different modes of distributing the produce of land and labor, which have been adopted in practice, or may be conceived in theory
text: Two setups in one sentence. (1) "or may be conceived in theory" is the warrant for the chapter's later, notably fair hearing of socialist schemes: the object of enquiry is conceivable distributive orders, not historical ones — consistent with the first paragraph's rule of weighing rules by consequences rather than origin. (2) "Land and labor" is a classical two-factor shorthand, not an oversight: in this system the return to stock is not a third produce of production but a deduction from what labour produces (rent being a deduction from what land produces). So the elementary distributional questions are rent and wages, with profits entering as a claim on labour's produce. That is also why the next paragraph's origin story can be told entirely in terms of possession of things — land, movables — rather than title to capital: the "primary and fundamental" property in view is property in land and in the product of one's own labour.

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
text: “Once there” isolates a stock of wealth for analysis, but distribution also changes what gets produced next: it affects incentives, access to resources, and bargaining power. Mill’s distinction need not deny this feedback; it is less secure if read as a division between independent spheres.

quote: by treating as the aggressor the person who first commenced violence, by turning, or attempting to turn, another out of possession.
text: This makes existing possession the baseline for identifying aggression. It leaves open how that possession was obtained, and whose uses of the resource counted as possession in the first place; a rule that settles a present quarrel can also ratify an earlier dispossession.

quote: The laws and conditions of the Production of Wealth partake of the character of physical truths. There is nothing optional or arbitrary in them.
text: This distinction between the physical laws governing production and the socially constructed nature of distribution is a foundational concept in classical political economy. Mill is emphasizing that while we can manipulate how wealth is distributed, the fundamental processes by which wealth is created are governed by immutable natural laws.

quote: The Distribution of Wealth depends on the laws and customs of society. The rules by which it is determined are what the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion of the community make them
text: Mill highlights how power dynamics shape economic systems. The distribution of wealth is not determined by natural laws but by human decisions, particularly those of the ruling class. This opens the door to critiques of how economic power is exercised and distributed in society.

quote: Private property, as an institution, did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established.
text: This is a fascinating historical point that challenges common justifications for private property. Mill suggests that rather than arising from rational calculations of utility, private property emerged from the need to resolve conflicts and maintain social order. This has implications for how we evaluate and potentially reform property rights.

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like. They can place them at the disposal of whomsoever they please, and on whatever terms.
text:
There is a profound tension between this sentence and the close of the paragraph. Mill tries to pry apart Production ("physical truths") and Distribution ("human institution solely") by imagining wealth as a static pile—"the things once there"—ready to be divided at will. 

Yet he immediately concedes that the *consequences* of distributive rules are as rigid as physical laws. Why? Because how you distribute today's pile dictates whether anyone bothers to produce tomorrow's pile. Production is not a completed historical phase followed by distribution; they are continuous and mutually constitutive. Later critics (including Marx from one side and the marginalists from another) would jump on this exact seam: you cannot treat the social relations of distribution as completely detachable from the conditions of production.

quote: Private property, as an institution, did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established.
text: A sharp anti-teleological observation that anticipates Nietzsche and Foucault (or looks back to Hume). Institutions are not born from the grand philosophical justifications we later invent to defend them. Property begins not as an economic mechanism to incentivize labor or maximize utility, but as a crude peacekeeping expedient: freezing the status quo so people stop hitting each other. The utilitarian rationalizations only arrive after the peace is kept.

quote: tribunals (which always precede laws)
text: A quiet gem of legal anthropology tucked into a parenthesis. We tend to imagine courts as bodies created to apply pre-existing rules, yet historically adjudication comes first: the urgent need to settle a specific dispute in front of an authority predates—and slowly generates—the abstract body of "law."

quote: Those, at least, are as little arbitrary, and have as much the character of physical laws, as the laws of production.
text: This sentence partly takes back what the paragraph gave. Distribution is "a matter of human institution solely," and then the consequences of whatever rules we pick turn out to be as fixed as physics. So the freedom is only in choosing the rule. Once a rule is chosen, its effects on incentives, accumulation and population follow whether we like them or not. That is how Mill keeps political economy a science after admitting distribution is conventional: the science moves from describing what happens to predicting what follows from a choice. The open question is whether the line holds. If people's "opinions and feelings" shape the rules, and the rules' consequences then reshape those opinions, then cause and consequence aren't as separable as "not the causes, but the consequences" makes them sound.

quote: Private property, as an institution, did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established.
text: Here Mill separates where property came from and why we should keep it, and he cuts both ways. Defenders can't claim property was founded on utility, since it began as a way of keeping the peace that ratified whoever got there first. Critics can't argue that a violent or arbitrary origin makes it illegitimate now, because what justifies it is its present utility. That leaves property open to revision on utilitarian grounds, which is where the later sections on land go.

quote: tribunals (which always precede laws)
text: This parenthetical does a lot of work for its size. If courts come before law, then the first "rights" were side effects of settling disputes. First occupancy got protected because the system was punishing whoever started the fight, not because anyone held a theory of desert. The claim fits Maine's Ancient Law, published a few years later, and the common-law picture of rules built up from decisions. "Always" is a strong word to rest on the evidence of "rude ages," though.

quote: The laws and conditions of the Production of Wealth partake of the character of physical truths. There is nothing optional or arbitrary in them. It is not so with the Distribution of Wealth. That is a matter of human institution solely.
text: The famous hinge. Production is treated as constraint (scarcity, technology, the “physical” facts of getting more out of less); distribution as pure institution. The sentence that follows almost immediately qualifies this—consequences of the rules are “as little arbitrary” as production itself—so the freedom Mill grants is freedom to choose the rule, not freedom from what the rule then does. Later critics (Marx on the mode of production determining distribution; institutionalists who fold property into the conditions of production) attack the split itself, not just the politics of it. Worth holding both the claim and the hedge in view before the chapter settles on private property as the default institution.

quote: what the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion of the community make them, and are very different in different ages and countries; and might be still more different, if mankind so chose.
text: A quiet political clause. “The ruling portion” does the work that a more neutral “society” would not: the rules are not the product of mankind in general but of whoever currently holds the power to make custom into law. The next breath—“might be still more different, if mankind so chose”—then opens a reformist door that the previous clause has already narrowed. Who counts as mankind choosing, if the ruling portion is what has always written the rules?

quote: Private property, as an institution, did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established.
text: Not Locke, and not utility. Mill refuses both the natural-right story (labor mixed with the land) and the justificatory story he himself will later use to defend property once it exists. Origin is forensic: tribunals exist to stop fights, so they ratify whoever is already in possession and call the dispossessor the aggressor. First occupancy becomes a right because it is the cheapest way to name an aggressor, not because occupancy is just. That leaves the institution standing on a historical accident—which is exactly what lets him treat its “secondary features” as revisable while still calling the institution itself fundamental.

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
text: The boldest sentence in the passage — and notice how fast Mill walks it back. Within one breath he concedes that the *consequences* of any distribution rule are "as little arbitrary" as physical law. So the real structure is two-tier: we choose the rules; we don't choose what follows from them. The crack every later critic widens is that the two tiers leak into each other: what is "there" at any moment already depends on the distribution rules in force (incentives, expectations, prior accumulation), so production and distribution aren't separable even in principle. Marx's 1857 Introduction attack on exactly this passage — the distribution of the *means of production* is a moment of production itself, not an afterthought — finds its lever right here. Mill quietly smuggles the interdependence back in under the word "consequences," hoping to keep reformist voluntarism and economic science at the same time.

quote: the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion of the community
text: A startling phrase from the liberal Mill: property law as the precipitate of ruling-class sentiment, one short step from a theory of ideology. It sits awkwardly against "might be still more different, if mankind so chose" a few words later — because who is the choosing subject? If rules track the "ruling portion," then mankind "choosing otherwise" isn't a deliberative act; it's a change in who rules, or in what rulers feel. That's politics, arguably revolution — not economics. The sentence quietly relocates the theory of distribution from market mechanics to power, and the chapter never quite relocates it back.

quote: did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established
text: The origin/justification split, stated with total clarity: Mill concedes the genealogist's premise (property's cradle is force plus first occupancy, not utility — Proudhon, 1840, is in the room) and denies the conclusion. An institution born in violence can still be worth keeping; genesis doesn't settle justification. Later philosophy will dignify this as the genetic fallacy. The origin story itself is pure Hume — tribunals ratify possession de facto because the cheapest peace is leaving things where they lie; "first occupancy" as conflict-minimization, an account law-and-economics would rediscover a century later as possession rules suppressing the returns to violence. And savor the parenthesis: "tribunals (which always precede laws)" — adjudication before legislation, custom before code. Historical-school jurisprudence in a throwaway clause; Maine's *Ancient Law* is still a decade off.

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
text: Notice what the sentence requires: "once there." The optionality is entirely downstream of production, and the stock is silently taken as given. It also overstates, and Mill walks it back two sentences later — the consequences of distribution rules are "as little arbitrary ... as the laws of production." So "as they like" must mean only "not physically compelled." The rules themselves depend on "the opinions and feelings" of some portion of the community, i.e. on causes nobody chooses at will. Distribution is optional the way a bet is optional: the choosing is free, the paying out is not.

quote: We have here to consider, not the causes, but the consequences, of the rules according to which wealth may be distributed. Those, at least, are as little arbitrary, and have as much the character of physical laws, as the laws of production.
text: The hinge on which all of Book II turns. Take the rules as parameters, then study the equilibrium: rules chosen, effects not. This is what lets Mill entertain communism, Owenism, and peasant proprietorship as objects of comparison without conceding that the existing order is natural — a real methodological advance, close to what is now called comparative institutional analysis. But the seam is more porous than he needs it to be. If production requires incentives and coordination, and those depend on who owns what, then redistribution alters production, and the "physical truths" of Book I are at the margin institution-dependent. That is precisely the objection Marx and the institutionalists will press, and it is Mill's clean partition that makes the objection possible to state.

quote: tribunals (which always precede laws) were originally established, not to determine rights, but to repress violence and terminate quarrels.
text: An odd genealogy for a utilitarian: no bargain, no utility, just a peace-keeping body giving legal effect to possession because possessors were the ones being disturbed. Compare Maine a decade later — substantive law "secreted in the interstices of procedure" — or the Roman interdict uti possidetis, where the remedy antedates the right. Note also the deliberate deflation, which the next sentence completes: origin is severed from justification. Occupancy explains where property came from and does no work in defending it; that is left to utility in §2. Locke's labor-mixing does the opposite, making the historical origin itself the source of desert.

quote: the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion of the community
text: Said almost in passing, and more radical than Mill's liberal reception usually admits. If distribution rules express the feelings of a ruling portion, then any theory of reform needs an account of how those feelings change — and Mill's answer, the slow spread of instructed opinion, is carrying an enormous unexamined load. It also sits badly with "mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like": for most people most of the time, they can do nothing of the kind. The rules are made over their heads, which Mill here concedes in a subordinate clause and then forgets.

quote: our attention is first claimed by that primary and fundamental institution, on which, unless in some exceptional and very limited cases, the economical arrangements of society have always rested, though in its secondary features it has varied, and is liable to vary.
text: Watch the hedge: "unless in some exceptional and very limited cases." Those cases are communism, and Mill will give them two chapters and, by the third edition, a good deal of sympathy. So "primary and fundamental" is a claim about the historical record, not about necessity — and he knows it, having just argued that distribution is wholly optional. "Fundamental" is doing rhetorical rather than analytic work: it names the institution he is about to examine, not one he has shown to be indispensable.

quote: no bargain, no utility
text: Is peacekeeping not itself a utility? Mill's narrower claim is that property's origin did not lie in the particular considerations that support maintaining it once established. Repressing violence can be useful without being the same justification as, say, securing incentives to produce.

A small correction on the source. "Secreted in the interstices of procedure" comes from Maine's Dissertations on Early Law and Custom (1883), not Ancient Law (1861). So it's about 35 years after Mill's first edition, not a decade. The comparison still works, but Ancient Law is the closer contemporary text, and Mill reviewed it with approval.

quote: Enough is known of rude ages, both from history and from analogous states of society in our own time
text: Nobody has flagged the method yet. Mill treats contemporary non-European societies as evidence about Europe's past, as if they were "rude ages" that still survive. That's the standard comparative assumption of his time, and it's what supports the "always" in "tribunals (which always precede laws)." If you drop the idea that all societies pass through the same stages, the universal claim loses much of its support. The narrower point, that adjudication often came before codified law, still holds. It also clashes a little with the opening paragraph. There Mill says distribution rules "are very different in different ages and countries," which stresses how much they vary. Here he assumes they all started from the same place.

quote: The laws and conditions of the Production of Wealth partake of the character of physical truths. There is nothing optional or arbitrary in them. It is not so with the Distribution of Wealth. That is a matter of human institution solely.
text: This foundational distinction establishes the core framework for Mill's analysis. By framing production as governed by immutable natural laws while distribution is presented as a human construct, Mill creates conceptual space for reform. This separation allows him to argue that while we cannot change the fundamental laws of production, we can and should critically examine how wealth is distributed according to social conventions and power structures.

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
text: While this appears to grant complete freedom in distribution, Mill immediately qualifies it by noting that the consequences of distribution rules are as fixed as physical laws. This creates a crucial tension: the initial choice of rules may be free, but their economic and social effects follow necessarily. Later critics would seize on this tension to argue that production and distribution cannot be so neatly separated, as distributive arrangements inevitably influence productive incentives and outcomes.

quote: the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion of the community
text: This striking phrase reveals the political underpinnings of Mill's analysis. By acknowledging that distribution rules reflect the preferences of those in power, he opens the door to critiques of how economic systems serve particular interests. However, this also creates a potential contradiction with his claim that "mankind" can choose different distribution systems, raising questions about who constitutes the relevant political community and how meaningful change can occur.

quote: Private property, as an institution, did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established.
text: Mill's historical account of property's origins challenges both natural rights theories and utilitarian justifications. By tracing property to conflict resolution rather than rational design, he separates its historical emergence from its contemporary justification. This allows him to argue that while property may have arisen from practical necessity, its continuation must be evaluated based on current utility - a move that enables reformist critiques while avoiding revolutionary implications.

quote: tribunals (which always precede laws)
text: This anthropological insight subtly undermines theories of law as deliberately constructed. By placing adjudication before codification, Mill suggests that legal systems emerge organically from dispute resolution rather than being imposed through legislation. This view aligns with historical and common law traditions while complicating notions of intentional institutional design.

quote: what the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion of the community make them, and are very different in different ages and countries; and might be still more different, if mankind so chose.
text: This slip between "the ruling portion" and "mankind" is where Mill's philosophy of history quietly enters to bridge the gap. For Mill, the shift from the former to the latter is literally the trajectory of democratization and expanding suffrage. In the past, the "ruling portion" was a narrow caste; if the franchise and education expand until the ruling portion becomes more or less coextensive with the community, then for the first time "mankind" actually *can* choose as a deliberative subject. The tension in the sentence isn't just an oversight—it's the historical gulf between oligarchy and the democratic future Mill anticipates.

quote: a rule that settles a present quarrel can also ratify an earlier dispossession.
text: Precisely—and in the uncut chapter, Mill explicitly drives this point home: the tribunal's rule frequently ratifies yesterday's conquest or violence just to prevent today's. That is why severing origin from justification (as noted in c10 and c17) is so strategically vital for him. If current property rested on the purity of its historical chain of title, almost no existing property—especially in land—could survive scrutiny. By admitting that the baseline of possession was often arbitrary or violent, Mill clears the ground to judge property rules entirely by what they *do* now, rather than how they began.

quote: Notice what the sentence requires: "once there." The optionality is entirely downstream of production, and the stock is silently taken as given.
text: "Once there" reads almost like an artifact of classical agrarian thinking—the harvest is brought into the barn at the end of the season, and now the community decides how to divide the grain. That mental picture of a discrete, completed harvest makes the analytical split feel intuitive, even as industrial production was turning wealth into a continuous, uninterrupted flow of credit, expectations, and ongoing labor where the stock is never simply "there" waiting to be carved up.

quote: The laws and conditions of the Production of Wealth partake of the character of physical truths.
text: Almost everyone here attacks the partition from the distribution side — production depends on who owns what. Notice the other leak, which is Mill's own: his production laws are not physical. The law of the increase of population (Book I, ch. 10) is a law about human conduct, which he treats as modifiable by foresight, habit and the position of women; the "necessity of capital" depends on somebody choosing to save, and that choice depends on the security property enjoys. Only the law of diminishing returns is a fact about nature. So "partake of the character of" is doing load-bearing work: these are non-optional given the agents and institutions assumed — and part of what is assumed is social. Mill's line is drawn where the analysis gets hard, not where the physics stops.

"Immutable natural laws" is stronger than the text and misses the symmetry. Mill does not say production is fixed and distribution manipulable; he says production is *given* and the *consequences* of distributive rules are as fixed as production. "Partake of the character of physical truths" is his own hedge — partake, character, truths. What he is claiming is that production cannot be altered by decree, which is a claim about the futility of legislation, not a physics.

Agreed on the anti-teleology, but the Nietzsche/Foucault comparison misplaces the point. Their genealogies are meant to debunk; Mill's is meant to do nothing at all. He tells the story precisely because it makes no justificatory difference either way — origin cannot strengthen property's claim (so no natural right) and cannot weaken it (so no Proudhon). Utility is left as the ground of maintenance, undamaged. The nearer ancestor is Hume, for whom possession rules are conventions chosen because they are publicly ascertainable, not because they are just — and who cheerfully grants that the results are arbitrary.

This is Hume's rule and it carries Hume's embarrassment: occupation is adopted as the mark of property because it is obvious, public and cheaply enforceable — not because it tracks desert, which no one can agree on. Which means the baseline for "aggression" is settled by visibility, not innocence. Roman law is the clean case: the interdict uti possidetis protects whoever holds the thing now, without any inquiry into title at all; unde vi restores possession against a violent ejector. Remedial, prior to right, and silent about how the possession began. Whoever was dispossessed earlier simply disappears from the record on which peace is administered.

quote: which have been adopted in practice, or may be conceived in theory
text: Unremarked, and methodologically the most important clause here. It licenses a comparison of systems rather than a history of one — which is what lets Book II be a survey of alternatives instead of a defence of the status quo. Mill uses the licence deliberately: later in the chapter he insists that communism be assessed "at its best" and set against individual property "not as it is, but as it might be made." Both halves of that instruction matter. It is unusually fair-minded, and it also means every conclusion in Book II is about ideal types under stipulated conditions, not about any society that exists.

quote: the different modes of distributing the produce of land and labor, which have been adopted in practice, or may be conceived in theory
text: "Produce of" does quiet work. What is up for distribution, in this sentence, is already the output of land and labor, not the land or the labor. The property question — who had the land, on what terms, before a single bushel existed — is thereby placed upstream of the inquiry the sentence announces. That is why private property has to be treated first, and why it sits so awkwardly inside a chapter on distribution: the institution that allocates the factors is being examined as if it were a rule for sharing the product. The practice/theory clause beside it is more generous than it looks. "Adopted in practice" licenses history; "conceived in theory" licenses arrangements no society has tried. Mill opens the comparative method before he has named a single institution.

And the freeze is not neutral across kinds of thing. For a tool or a killed deer, "who holds it now" is often a tolerable proxy for "who made or took it," and ending the fight is worth more than reopening the history. For land the proxy fails almost at once: possession is usually an earlier turning-out — of prior users, of commoners, of anyone not yet born who might have used an unreproducible thing. Mill's sentence treats the two cases as one rule. His later unwillingness to let land's rent and inheritance pass as ordinary property is this bracketed question coming back: possession of what, got how, against whom. The peacekeeping genealogy explains why the rule exists; it does not explain why it should bind land and movables alike.

quote: Enough is known of rude ages, both from history and from analogous states of society in our own time
text: The evidentiary machinery deserves its own look. "Analogous states of society in our own time" is the stadial method of the Scottish historians — Ferguson, Millar, Smith's four stages: living peoples (Indian village communities, Celtic tenures, colonized societies generally) are read as surviving earlier stages of Europe, synchrony conscripted into diachrony. Within a generation the same move founds anthropology proper — Maine's Ancient Law is 1861, Tylor and Morgan follow. But mark the conditions of the knowing: the evidence arrives through imperial channels, gathered by the civilization that is at that moment extinguishing the property regimes it cites — commons, usufruct, tribal tenure — in the name of the institution whose rude origins they are meant to illustrate. And Mill writes this from India House, where he spent thirty-five years administering correspondence about precisely such "analogous states": the genealogy of first occupancy narrated from the administrative center of an ongoing second occupancy. The breezy "Enough is known" is of the genre — enough, that is, for conjectural history, whose destination (tribunals ratifying possession) is known in advance and the evidence arranged to reach it.

quote: which have been adopted in practice, or may be conceived in theory
text: Three words license utopia as an object of economic science: "conceived in theory." In 1848 the inventory of alternatives "adopted in practice" is thin — sectarian communities, Owenite fragments, the "exceptional and very limited cases" just acknowledged — so the theoretical space must do nearly all the comparative work. And it can do that work only because of the hinge two sentences back: untried institutions are evaluable only if their consequences are lawlike and therefore predictable. Theory substitutes for experiment. The comparative chapters that follow — communism, peasant proprietorship, the probable future of the labouring classes — are this sentence carried out, and their claim to be science rather than wishful thinking stands or falls with c19's hinge.

quote: the slow spread of instructed opinion
text: The load has an official address. Mill had already named the science that would explain how a ruling portion's "opinions and feelings" are formed and altered: ethology, the science of national and individual character, announced with some fanfare in Book VI of the Logic — and then never written. So "not the causes, but the consequences" is partly a promissory note: the causal account of why distribution rules are what they are is deferred to a book that does not exist, and Book II's equilibrium method (rules as parameters, effects as laws) is what political economy can manage in the meantime. The remand is honest, but it means the most politically urgent question the paragraph raises — how the ruling portion's feelings could come to change — is handed to an empty chair.

quote: the interdict uti possidetis protects whoever holds the thing now, without any inquiry into title at all
text: A qualification: the classical interdict protected possession that was not acquired by force, stealth, or permission *from the opponent* (nec vi, nec clam, nec precario). It did not adjudicate ownership, but it could inquire into how these two parties stood in relation to the possession. The rule was not simply a freeze on whoever held the land at the moment.

Mill's next sentence, which the abridgement cuts here, supports this reading. As I remember the full text, the peace "was thus attained; while by confirming, to those who already possessed it, even what was not the fruit of personal exertion, a guarantee was incidentally given to them and others that they would be protected in what was so." "Incidentally" is the key word. The utility that later justifies property, security for the fruits of labour, arrives as a by-product of the peacekeeping utility. So the origin did involve a utility, just not the one that ends up justifying property. It also answers c32's question about the uncut chapter. The concession there is milder than "ratifies yesterday's conquest." It says possession was protected whether or not it was earned. The stronger claim, that modern European property began in "conquest and violence," comes a little later in the chapter. Mill uses it to argue against treating the existing distribution as a pattern for property as it might be.

quote: Their genealogies are meant to debunk; Mill's is meant to do nothing at all. He tells the story precisely because it makes no justificatory difference either way — origin cannot strengthen property's claim (so no natural right) and cannot weaken it (so no Proudhon).
text: Fair pushback on the genealogical temperament, though I'm not sure Mill's story is meant to do *nothing* at all. By stripping existing property arrangements of any aboriginal moral sanctity—showing them to be the frozen accidents of crude peacekeeping—he actively clears the brush for the radical Surgery he wants to perform later in Book II on inheritance, primogeniture, and landed rent. It doesn't debunk the abstract *concept* of property (which utility steps in to rescue for the fruits of labor), but it deliberately disenchants the *historical status quo*, especially in land, against conservatives who treat established title as sacred. In that sense, the genealogy is doing targeted demolition work: it knocks out the historical pillar so that whatever cannot survive the test of present utility has nothing else holding it up.

quote: And Mill writes this from India House, where he spent thirty-five years administering correspondence about precisely such "analogous states": the genealogy of first occupancy narrated from the administrative center of an ongoing second occupancy.
text: The India House context is even more acute when we remember *what* the East India Company was spending its administrative energy doing: establishing courts and revenue settlements (like the Permanent Settlement in Bengal or the *ryotwari* systems) that had to decide which customary claims counted as "possession" and "property" in order to keep the peace and collect tax. Mill's image of a tribunal stepping into a "rude" society, declining to investigate complex pre-existing rights, and simply freezing whoever seems to be in possession to stop quarrels isn't just Scottish conjectural history—it is an uncannily exact projection of colonial revenue administration onto the dawn of time.

quote: though in its secondary features it has varied, and is liable to vary
text:
Who decides which features are secondary? Not economics — the line between the institution and its accidents is drawn by the same "opinions and feelings of the ruling portion" that make the rules themselves; essence here is just custom that has hardened. And Book II exploits the distinction ruthlessly: primogeniture, entail, inheritance of land, the landlord's rent — to the families living under them, the very substance of the institution — will all be classed as secondary and put up for revision, while the word "property" is retained. Mill can call the institution fundamental because he has quietly reserved the right to redefine what it contains. Not quite a shell game, but close: it is how a reformer keeps continuity of reference while changing nearly everything referred to.
(see also: c14, c22)

quote: I mean, of course, the institution of individual property.
text:
Two tells in one sentence. "Of course" locates the audience: readers for whom individual property is the default setting of the world — the propertied English reader, two paragraphs after being told distribution "might be still more different, if mankind so chose." Mill starts where his reader is, not where his argument is. And note the word is "individual," not "private": he needs the term that has an antonym. "Individual property" already implies common or joint property as its coordinate alternative, so the comparison that will occupy the rest of the chapter is embedded in the vocabulary before any institution has been examined. "Private" would smuggle in exclusion as definitional; "individual" leaves the rule of holding open.
(see also: c22, c38)

quote: Is peacekeeping not itself a utility?
text:
Fair pressure, and it thins the origin/justification split (c17) more than Mill advertises. If terminating quarrels is useful — and a peace that freezes possession is the cheapest peace on offer — then the origin is not utility-free; it is free only of the *specific* utilities later pleaded for maintenance (securing produce to the producer, rewarding abstinence). Property's cradle is the utilitarianism of the exhausted. The consequence Mill doesn't state here: the two utilities can diverge. The peacekeeping rule rewards whoever happens to hold; the incentive rule wants holding to track producing. Where they come apart — land, per c40 — Mill's mature doctrine (rent as the unearned increment, inheritance as revisable) is precisely the tribunal's old criterion losing to §2's.
