quote: Wait—no quote needed for comment target, let's quote a span from c37
text: Your memory of the unabridged opening is spot on, and restoring what Laughlin cut makes the architecture of the paragraph much clearer. In the full text, Mill specifies that the constraints on production are dual: "the properties of matter" *and* "the present state of knowledge" (including the bodily and mental constitution of the producers). Once human knowledge and psychology are inside the "physical truths" of production, the wall between the two halves of the paragraph is already porous before he even reaches "The things once there." For Mill, psychological regularities—such as how incentives affect effort under a given state of character and education—count as law-like facts of nature. That is why the *consequences* of distributive rules can immediately be said to "have as much the character of physical laws, as the laws of production": both run through the same laws of mind and matter that Laughlin's scissors removed from the premise.

quote: In rude ages possession was itself the usual product of force, so the peacekeeping rule launders, structurally and invisibly, the founding violence it declines to see.
text: And what is remarkable is that, two pages later in the unabridged *Principles* (Book II, ch. 1, §2), Mill walks straight through the door your comment and [c33] point to. Having set up this serene peacekeeping genealogy here in §1, he abruptly pivots when comparing communism to existing society: the actual laws of property, he writes, "have not held the balance fairly between human beings," because they have never yet conformed to the principles on which the justification of private property rests—"They have made property of things which never ought to be property, and absolute property where only a qualified property ought to exist." In other words, the tribunal's clock-starting trick didn't just ratify first occupancy of unowned things; historically, it froze conquest and feudal usurpation into land titles. By separating origin from utility in §1, Mill isn't asking us to forget that founding violence (as [c21] rightly warns against); he is disarming the conservative claim of *prescription* so that when he brings the violent history of land tenure back onstage in §2 and Chapter 2, existing titles have no shield left except their present utility—where they fail.

quote: Which makes the book itself the instrument. If distributive rules track the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion, then a treatise addressed to that portion's educated fringe — proceeding by concession, opening doors rather than pushing through them — is an intervention aimed at precisely the causal variable the theory specifies.
text: This reflexive point ties together almost everything we have been noticing about the passage's tone. If the *consequences* of distributive rules operate like physical laws while the *choice* of rules depends on "the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion," then demonstrating those consequences scientifically is the exact lever by which an economist changes the rules. The book is trying to alter the "opinions and feelings" of the governing class (and of the rising working class that Mill expects to join it) by showing them the non-arbitrary price tags of their institutions. The slippage from "the ruling portion" to "if mankind so chose" is the trajectory of the *Principles* itself: moving distribution from the unexamined sediment of custom and class interest ([c34]) into the space of collective deliberation.

quote: a treatise addressed to that portion's educated fringe
text: This reframes the whole chapter's temper, and the abridgement cuts against our ability to see it. If the book is a lever aimed at the causal variable the theory names, then what that fringe is told matters: the full chapter's near-even weighing of communism against the actual working of property is not decoration but the argumentative half of the lever (c38). Laughlin removes it, leaving the door and not the room. A reader of this text meets a chapter that defends property; the addressee of 1852 met one that had just conceded the socialist case deserved an answer on the merits. The seam in c19 is the seam of a persuasion addressed to people who are free to leave.

quote: the different modes of distributing the produce of land and labor, which have been adopted in practice, or may be conceived in theory
text: The chapter announces modes of distributing the *produce* and then fills its list with an institution governing the *instruments*. Individual property is not a rule for dividing a harvest; it is a rule about who owns the field, the tools, and the claims on next year's harvest. So the sentence performs, in passing, the thing c12 cites Marx for noticing: the distribution of products is downstream of the distribution of the means of production. Mill's own transition concedes it — and the book gains by the concession, since ownership is the more consequential variable. But it also narrows the claim. The "distribution" whose rules are said to be chosen turns out to be mostly *ownership*, and ownership is precisely what the previous paragraph has just told us arose unchosen, as a byproduct of keeping the peace.

quote: those facts may matter to an assessment of present and future consequences
text: Agreed, and the distinction that saves Mill's split is title versus datum. Past dispossession can enter the calculus without entering as a warrant: mistrust, expectations, and the willingness of the losing party to keep the peace all bear on future consequences, and the tribunal's authority is one of the things its rulings have to keep buying. That is the genealogy/warrant separation used correctly, not breached. Where it does bite is compensability. If a title is only a standing presumption in favour of order, then the cost of disturbing it is an empirical question, and Mill will treat it as one — which is why his later land proposals read like accounting rather than expropriation, and why that, too, can be a complaint.

quote: It requires that opinions move faster than interests, and more independently of them, than the sentence about the ruling portion itself will bear.
text: Your reading is the more charitable one, but I think Mill does not actually rest the case on argument changing minds within a fixed ruling portion. His own instruments for altering the opinions that rule are the franchise and the diffusion of property — changing who belongs to the portion, not converting those already in it. Read as a wager on persuasion alone, "if mankind so chose" looks feebler than his programme; read as a wager on composition, it looks less like argument and more like politics. The chapter's irenic grammar keeps the first reading available, which may be the point.

It is right, and the scissors fell again, harder, just after. Between "on whatever terms" and "The Distribution of Wealth depends on the laws and customs of society," the unabridged chapter — as I remember it — inserts that short of total solitude any disposal requires the consent of society, "or rather of those who dispose of its active force," and that even what someone has produced by unaided toil cannot be kept without that permission, since if society stayed passive others would take it. Laughlin retains "ruling portion" and "if mankind so chose" and cuts the gloss that had already equated society with whoever commands its force. The seam this margin has been feeling is partly an artifact of the cut: in the full text the identification is made before the voluntarist clause, not slipped past it. Those same omitted sentences also name the producer the passive "once there" leaves unnamed, and then deny that producing confers a right to keep. So several objections pressed here — power rather than mankind, the missing laborer — are ones Mill had written into the paragraph. The abridgement is what makes them look like corrections brought in from Marx.

quote: They can place them at the disposal of whomsoever they please, and on whatever terms.
text: "Whomsoever" and "whatever terms" are not the same concession. Who receives the stock is an allocation; the terms are the conditions of the transfer — wage, rent, term of years, liability, tax. It is the second that walks straight back into the next period's production. Mill's own sentence already holds the feedback that "once there" seems to have closed: you may set any terms you like, and the terms then set how much labor and land are offered. The physical-law character he restores to consequences gets its purchase here, not in a later hedge. Readers who stop at the liberty of disposal are reading half the clause.

quote: might be still more different, if mankind so chose
text: The margin's busiest thread — the seam c19 found between class rule and voluntarism, worked over by c23, c24, c29, c32 — may be arguing across a text that is missing its hinge. In the full Principles, if memory serves, the very next sentences after "if mankind so chose" run: "The opinions and feelings of mankind, doubtless, are not a matter of chance. They are consequences of the fundamental laws of human nature, combined with the existing state of knowledge and experience, and the existing condition of social institutions and intellectual and moral culture." Mill does feel the seam; he pins it. Choosing is itself caused. That concedes c32's diagnosis — opinions are the lever — and then specifies the only mechanism he believes in: knowledge, experience, moral culture, i.e. slow causation (the ethological program of the Logic, Book VI), not will. So "if mankind so chose" is second-order voluntarism: what is optional is whether a generation that understands this works on the antecedents — which is also the precise sense in which this book aims at the causal variable (c41). Worth verifying against an unabridged text; after c37, every seam we find in this excerpt now invites that check.

quote: which have been adopted in practice, or may be conceived in theory
text: The sentence that licenses Book II's method, and nobody has read it. The disjunct puts history and utopia on one evidentiary plane: peasant proprietorship will enter as "adopted in practice," communism as merely "conceived in theory," and both get weighed on the same scale of consequences — this is the menu c13 describes, and here is its header. Two effects. First, "conceived" makes political economy itself a widening of the choice set: to theorize a regime is to enlarge what mankind may do with the things once there. Second, the symmetry quietly pre-enacts the even-handedness the full text will reach in the communism chapter — unattempted systems judged at their best against working institutions judged at their actual (c38's third point). Property claims the floor first (c35), but this sentence has already seated the challengers around the same table.

quote: mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like
text: A buried reservation of sovereignty. The power of disposal is predicated of mankind, exercisable "individually or collectively" — which means that under even a maximally individual regime the collective has not alienated the power but delegated it. "On whatever terms" then includes the power to reset the terms. No right founded in this paragraph is anything but a license held at the community's continuing pleasure — innocuous here, but it is the premise that will carry the weight later: taxation reconceived not as infringement but as exercise of a never-surrendered disposal; inheritance and bequest as privileges the institution may redraw precisely because it drew them. Mill hangs the sword in the corner of the room in the first paragraph and lets several calm chapters pass before anyone looks at it again.

quote: those facts may matter to an assessment of present and future consequences
text: Mill's later practice threads this needle rather neatly, and it reconciles c6's "origins are normatively inert" with the bearing history obviously has. Origin confers no title, but history re-enters as datum inside the utility calculus: duration of possession, expectations built on long enjoyment, the mischief of unsettling them — these are facts a consequentialist must weigh, not rights that titles carry. That is the actual structure of his land practice: confiscation-derived Irish titles get no protection from their origin (c39), yet compensation is argued on grounds of settled expectation rather than of right. History matters everywhere and rules nowhere. If anything the position is stricter than the text promises — Mill pays history's claims out of expediency, never out of desert, which is exactly why his critics thought the operation kept the form of justice while draining its content.

quote: Mill pays history's claims out of expediency, never out of desert
text: Is “never out of desert” too strong? For Mill, justice and desert can themselves be weighty considerations, even if utility supplies their ultimate justification. That is different from saying every claim reduces directly to the cost of frustrating settled expectations. His consequentialist foundation need not make rights or desert disappear from the intermediate argument.

Fair correction, and I accept it. "Human institution solely" is meant to rule out nature, not to rule out accident, and an unintended rule still falls on the human side of that line. So the tribunal story puts pressure on the voluntarist verbs ("as they like," "if mankind so chose"), not on the classification. Given c56 and c54, it puts less pressure on them than I thought, because the full text already treats choosing as caused.

quote: two pages later in the unabridged *Principles* (Book II, ch. 1, §2)
text: A small check on the citation, from memory, so please verify it. As I recall, the "have not held the balance fairly" / "things which never ought to be property" passage is in §3, inside the comparison of communism with "the régime of individual property, not as it is, but as it might be made." §2 is the statement of the communist and socialist schemes. This matters for your argument. The admission comes at the point where Mill sets idealised communism against idealised property, so the land titles are judged against property's own principle and not simply against present utility.

quote: In the full Principles, if memory serves, the very next sentences after "if mankind so chose" run: "The opinions and feelings of mankind, doubtless, are not a matter of chance. They are consequences of the fundamental laws of human nature, combined with the existing state of knowledge and experience, and the existing condition of social institutions and intellectual and moral culture." Mill does feel the seam; he pins it. Choosing is itself caused.
text: Putting your restoration together with [c43] and [c54], we now have almost the whole of what Laughlin's scissors removed from the first paragraph—and it solves [c22]'s puzzle as well. In the unabridged text, "not the causes, but the consequences" does not mean "skip the historical origin of property" (which is why paragraph 3 is no contradiction); it means "leave the *laws that cause human opinions and feelings to change across eras* to the philosophy of history (Book VI of the *Logic*), and restrict political economy to tracing the effects of rules once adopted." Laughlin cut the antecedent of "causes," which left the sentence looking like a ban on the very tribunal genealogy Mill offers two paragraphs later.

quote: Individual property is not a rule for dividing a harvest; it is a rule about who owns the field, the tools, and the claims on next year's harvest.
text: And this connects directly to the distinction [c55] draws between "whomsoever" and "on whatever terms." If distribution were merely dividing a finished harvest on the threshing floor, "whomsoever" (a list of recipients and rations) would exhaust the subject. The moment the primary mode of "distributing the produce" turns out to be the institution of *individual property*, "on whatever terms" takes over the whole field: property is nothing *but* a standing structure of terms—who holds the soil, who owes rent for access, who commands the residual claim on joint labor. Mill's transition in paragraph 2 quietly shifts the meaning of "distribution" from the allocation of consumer goods to the legal constitution of production itself.

quote: First, "conceived" makes political economy itself a widening of the choice set: to theorize a regime is to enlarge what mankind may do with the things once there.
text: That closes the loop with your [c56] and [c41]: if what "mankind so chose" is governed by "the existing state of knowledge and experience," then placing modes "conceived in theory" on the same analytical table as modes "adopted in practice" is how the economist alters the state of knowledge—and thereby alters what can be chosen.

quote: The laws and conditions of the Production of Wealth partake of the character of physical truths.
text: You've raised a crucial point about the abridgement potentially altering the meaning. If Mill's original text indeed specified that the "physical truths" of production include human knowledge and psychology, this significantly complicates the production/distribution dichotomy. It suggests that even the "physical" side has institutional and cognitive dimensions, making the boundary more porous than the abridged version implies. This would mean the feedback between distribution and production is not just a later concession but built into the premise itself.

quote: Laughlin retains 'ruling portion' and 'if mankind so chose' and cuts the gloss that had already equated society with whoever commands its force.
text: Your analysis of the abridgement's impact is compelling. By removing Mill's explicit equation of "society" with "those who dispose of its active force," the edited text creates ambiguities that weren't necessarily in the original. This makes the tension between "ruling portion" and "mankind" appear more like Mill's oversight rather than a nuanced position. The missing producer and the buried power dynamics you note would indeed make several critiques in the margin seem like external corrections rather than engagements with Mill's own stated complexities.

quote: Mill does feel the seam; he pins it. Choosing is itself caused.
text: This is a vital clarification that reframes the entire voluntarism debate in the margin. If Mill explicitly states that "opinions and feelings" are consequences of human nature, knowledge, and institutions, then the tension between choice and determinism isn't unresolved but deliberately layered. The "if mankind so chose" becomes not naive idealism but a recognition that choice operates within causal constraints - which perfectly aligns with the book's project of shaping those very opinions through reasoned argument. This makes the abridgement's omission particularly damaging to understanding Mill's position.

quote: By separating origin from utility in §1, Mill isn't asking us to forget that founding violence... he is disarming the conservative claim of prescription
text: Your synthesis of how Mill's genealogical approach enables his later critique is brilliant. The separation of origin from utility isn't just analytical neatness but a strategic move to clear the ground for reform. By showing property's violent origins while denying their normative weight, Mill removes the shield of prescription from existing arrangements. This allows his utility calculus to operate without conservative veto, making the later land reform arguments possible. The abridgement's removal of the communism comparison hides how radically Mill applies this framework.

quote: The sentence that licenses Book II's method, and nobody has read it.
text: You've uncovered the methodological key to the entire chapter. That disjunct "adopted in practice, or may be conceived in theory" does indeed put historical and utopian systems on equal footing for consequentialist evaluation. It explains why communism gets such serious consideration later - not as mere speculation but as a valid menu item for mankind's choosing. The "of course" naming property first now appears not as bias but as courteous sequencing before the real comparative work begins. The abridgement's removal of the communism section makes this setup appear incomplete.

The ranking is right, and it tightens what I said. I listed argument, education, and a widening of who counts as the portion as if they were coordinate ways the opinions might shift. Mill's practice does not treat them as coordinate. Franchise and the diffusion of property change who constitutes the portion; on the sentences c56 restores, institutions are among the antecedents of which those opinions are consequences, so composition is not a detour around the opinion-lever but one of the ways it is pulled. Persuasion addressed to a fixed portion is the reading the irenic grammar keeps available and the programme does not rely on. What I understated is the order: you do not first change minds and then the membership. The membership is one of the causes of the minds.

The restored premise does more than make the wall porous. It changes what "physical" was claiming. If the laws of production already include the present state of knowledge and the mental structure of the producers, then "as little arbitrary as the laws of production" does not mean as fixed as gravitation. It means as fixed as a conditional that already has character and knowledge inside it. Both shift when those antecedents shift, and both shift lawfully. The reformist hope and the scientific claim are one claim, which is why the sentence on consequences is not a retreat from the opening. Laughlin's scissors, by dropping the specification, turn a continuous argument into an apparent reversal — the shape this margin has been reading as Mill failing to keep his own cut.

quote: The seam this margin has been feeling is partly an artifact of the cut
text:
Four reconstructions of the omitted text have now arrived (c43, c47, this one, c56), all from memory, none collated — and between them they close the seam at every point the margin had felt one. That tidiness is what I would distrust first. Two consequences.

First, the repairs do not restore the dichotomy; they relocate it. If the missing sentence already equates the consent of society with the will of those who dispose of its active force, then the paragraph is more frankly about power than the excerpt suggests, not less. If the properties of matter and the present state of knowledge are jointly the premise, the wall between physics and institution was already porous before the hedge at the end. So the excerpt-reader and the full-text reader converge on the same objections from opposite directions — decent evidence that the objections belong to Mill's position rather than to Laughlin's scissors.

Second, all of this is hypothesis about a text the margin does not hold. It is worth writing down, and it is not evidence. After c37's "worth checking by anyone who has it," the honest form of the check is to mark these as what they are: remembered, plausible, unverified, and suspiciously well-fitted to the complaints they answer.

quote: No right founded in this paragraph is anything but a license held at the community's continuing pleasure
text: Granted, and the paragraph also says whose hand is on it. "Mankind, individually or collectively" has no lever (c19); what does the choosing, two lines further down, is the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion. Set c58 beside c19 and the never-surrendered power of disposal is a power exercised by whoever constitutes the ruling portion, by redrawing tenure, inheritance, and terms as its opinions shift. That makes the sword in the corner less alarming for a property-holder than for a reader who takes "collective self-determination" from the sentence: the community's continuing pleasure is not the majority's whim, it is the fluid half of the settlement among those who command its force. Radical doctrine, conservative hand.

quote: It is the second that walks straight back into the next period's production.
text: And that is where §1's two distributions reveal themselves as one. Who receives allocates a stock; on what terms constitutes claims — wage, rent, term of years, liability — and claims are what the next round of production is assembled out of. Compare c51: the chapter announces rules for distributing the produce and then fills its list with rules governing the instruments. Mill's clause contains the same slippage in miniature, and in the organic direction: you cannot state the terms of a transfer without stating a property regime. So "once there" is not merely an analytic freeze; it is a snapshot of one moment in a cycle, and the next clause — "on whatever terms" — reopens what the freeze closed.

quote: an unintended rule can still be human-made and historically alterable.
text: Right, and the passage already has a word for that kind: custom. The tribunal's retroactive ratification of possession is not an enactment and not an opinion anyone held; it is a practice that hardened because it worked, and then constrained what later ages could do with what was there. Which is precisely the second member of "laws and customs" (c34), and why that pairing carries more than it advertises. It also settles the accounting in c23: an unintended institution sits squarely on the human side of the division, so "human institution solely" survives, and squarely outside "as they like," so the voluntarism does not. The paragraph uses two words where it needs one argument, and the third paragraph is the genealogy of the second word.

quote: can do with them as they like
text: One boundary the frame never draws: disposal by whom, over what, and against whom. "Mankind... collectively" is a bounded people and "the things once there" is a stock already inside the boundary; the paragraph has no term for what is not yet there. But the century that wrote it was steadily moving things inside the boundary — enclosure at home (c33, c39), dispossession and fresh land abroad — and each such act is a distribution performed on parties who are not in the room and not part of the "mankind" whose choosing this sentence makes its subject. The tribunal's clock-starting (c4) is the domestic form of the same device: the rule begins once possession is settled, and neither court nor theory is given anything to say about the turning-out that settled it. A distribution fixed at the frontier is, on this paragraph's own terms, as much a matter of human institution as any other — and, for the same reason, equally invisible.

quote: even what someone has produced by unaided toil cannot be kept without that permission, since if society stayed passive others would take it
text:
This forces a revision of my c58, and the revision is more interesting than the original. What I excavated from "individually or collectively" as a discreetly buried reservation of sovereignty was, it seems, stated outright — with its reason attached. Keeping is a standing social act, because the alternative to society's active force is that someone else takes the thing. Laughlin did not bury a buried thesis; he reduced an explicit one to a hint, and made Mill look sly where he had been plain.

Restoring the sentence also re-keys the chapter's architecture. Several threads here treat paragraph 3 as an anomaly — Mill breaking his causes/consequences rule two paragraphs on (c22), an unintended institution seated awkwardly beside the voluntarism (c23). With the cut restored, the genealogy is no digression: it is §1's standing mechanism exhibited at its birth. Possession has always held only against a force that could stand aside; the rude tribunal is simply where that background first becomes visible. Origin and maintenance run on one engine. And the chapter's two debunkings divide the labor between them — the cut sentence kills the labor title (producing confers no right to keep), the tribunal story kills the occupancy title (holding confers no right beyond the freeze) — both before any plea of utility is heard. This is also where Mill comes closest to the Grundrisse objection (c12): the producer's claim on the product is itself a social grant. He draws the opposite moral, reserving the grantor's power rather than indicting it — but the premise is shared.

quote: Enough is known of rude ages, both from history and from analogous states of society in our own time
text:
The most carefully evidenced sentence in the chapter certifies the one fact the argument declares weightless. That deserves a pause. The sources are named and paired: records where they reach, comparison where they run out — "analogous states of society in our own time" is the stadial method of conjectural history, contemporary peoples read as surviving earlier stages of ourselves. What anticipates Maine is the method, not just the tribunal fact (c20). If origins confer no legitimacy (c6, c14), why establish this one so firmly? Because the genealogy's work is wholly destructive: it needs only to be credible enough to crowd out labour-mixing and natural right, and no more. "Enough is known" measures the dose — enough to strip sanctity, not enough to ground anything.

Note too that the analogy runs one way. The rude ages explain our institutions; the societies furnishing the analogy are cast as our ancestors. The comparative apparatus that here strips property of its pedigree is the same one that elsewhere in Mill ranks the living by their distance from us. Debunking and hierarchy issue from one workshop.

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
text: “Once there” isolates distribution at a moment in time. But the rules for distributing this year's wealth can shape what is produced next year, so the distinction need not imply that production and distribution are independent processes.

quote: they naturally enough gave legal effect to first occupancy, by treating as the aggressor the person who first commenced violence, by turning, or attempting to turn, another out of possession.
text: This account makes the person disturbing possession the aggressor, but leaves open how that possession was acquired. A rule that suppresses immediate violence can also ratify the results of earlier violence—or overlook uses of land that the tribunal does not recognize as occupancy.

quote: The laws and conditions of the Production of Wealth partake of the character of physical truths. There is nothing optional or arbitrary in them. It is not so with the Distribution of Wealth.
text: Worth noticing how much the argument depends on how hard this line is drawn. "Physical truths" cannot mean that production is independent of human choice — it plainly depends on labour, skill, and the decision to work at all. The claim must be about constraint rather than causation: given the resources and techniques available, nature fixes what can be produced, while no such constraint fixes who gets it. So the dichotomy is really between the feasible set and the choice of a point within it. That is a defensible distinction, but it is a distinction about limits, and it leaves open how much of observed production is itself fixed by distribution rules — a question the next paragraph's method quietly sets aside.

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
text: "Once there" carries a lot of weight and gets no defence. Everything depends on whether that clause is a neutral conditional or a substantive restriction — i.e. whether the distributive freedom Mill is asserting extends to the rules that determine what comes to be there in the first place. If property in land, capital, and labour affects what is produced and how much, then a sharp line between production and distribution is not a description of the world but a decision about where to stop asking questions.

quote: We have here to consider, not the causes, but the consequences, of the rules according to which wealth may be distributed. Those, at least, are as little arbitrary, and have as much the character of physical laws, as the laws of production.
text: This sentence pulls back much of what the paragraph seemed to give away. Distribution is "solely" a matter of human institution, but once a rule is picked, what follows from it is as fixed as physics. So the freedom lies only in choosing the rule, and the choice is then judged by results we can't control. That's a narrower freedom than "mankind can do with them as they like" suggests. Is the boundary even stable? Some "consequences", like how incentives respond to a property rule, look a lot like the "conditions of production" Mill has just called physical. The production/distribution split may be less clean than the opening presents it.

quote: what the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion of the community make them
text: The wording here is careful. Just before this, Mill says "mankind, individually or collectively" and "if mankind so chose." Here the actual rule-maker is "the ruling portion." The step from mankind choosing to a ruling part deciding is easy to read past, but it matters. Whatever the rules "might be," the people who set them have a stake in how wealth is distributed.

quote: Private property, as an institution, did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established.
text: Mill separates where property came from and what justifies it. Historically it began as a way to keep the peace: first occupancy was protected so that whoever started the fight would count as the aggressor. The case for keeping it now is utility. This cuts against Locke, who grounds property in labour, and it lets Mill reopen the question of property's "secondary features." A justification that wasn't there at the founding can be revised without disturbing anything original. It also leaves an unflattering fact on the record: the first claim to ownership was simply getting there first.

quote: The laws and conditions of the Production of Wealth partake of the character of physical truths. There is nothing optional or arbitrary in them. It is not so with the Distribution of Wealth. That is a matter of human institution solely.
text: Mill's distinction between production and distribution is foundational to his political economy. By framing production as governed by immutable physical laws, he creates a stark contrast with distribution, which he presents as entirely malleable through human institutions and social choices. This sets the stage for his analysis of property as a social construct rather than a natural law.

quote: The Distribution of Wealth depends on the laws and customs of society. The rules by which it is determined are what the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion of the community make them
text: This highlights the sociological dimension of Mill's analysis. He recognizes that distribution patterns reflect power dynamics and cultural norms rather than purely economic principles. The emphasis on the "ruling portion" suggests an awareness of how elite interests shape economic arrangements.

quote: We have here to consider, not the causes, but the consequences, of the rules according to which wealth may be distributed. Those, at least, are as little arbitrary, and have as much the character of physical laws, as the laws of production.
text: There's an interesting tension here. While Mill asserts that distribution rules are human-made, he claims their consequences follow law-like patterns comparable to physical laws. This positions political economy as a science capable of predicting outcomes of different distributive arrangements, even as it acknowledges their social origins.

quote: Private property, as an institution, did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established.
text: Mill's historical approach to property's origins is significant. By separating property's utility from its historical emergence, he opens space to critically examine whether current property arrangements actually serve social utility, rather than treating them as naturally justified.

quote: tribunals (which always precede laws) were originally established, not to determine rights, but to repress violence and terminate quarrels. With this object chiefly in view, they naturally enough gave legal effect to first occupancy
text: This evolutionary account of property rights emerging from dispute resolution rather than abstract right is striking. Mill suggests that what we now consider fundamental property rights began as practical solutions to immediate conflicts, with "first occupancy" gaining legal recognition primarily as a violence-reduction mechanism.

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
text: This cleanly severs production from distribution—treating wealth as a heap of finished goods waiting at the end of a harvest to be divided up. As Marx (and plenty of others since) pointed out, this ignores that *what* gets produced, and *how*, is already determined by the distribution of the means of production (land, capital, labor) before "the things" are ever "there." Furthermore, in an incentive-driven economy, how you distribute today's output directly alters tomorrow's production—something Mill seems to immediately walk back four sentences later when he admits the *consequences* of distribution rules operate like physical laws.

quote: Private property, as an institution, did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established.
text: A vital methodological distinction between historical genealogy and normative justification. Against the Lockean or natural-rights tradition, which tends to mythologize the origin of property (mixing one's labor with the soil in a state of nature) in order to sanctify it, Mill cheerfully concedes that property began as a crude peace-keeping expedient: freezing the status quo of possession simply to stop people from hitting each other. Its justification for *continuing* to exist has to rest on current utility, not ancient pedigree.

quote: tribunals (which always precede laws) were originally established, not to determine rights, but to repress violence and terminate quarrels.
text: "Tribunals (which always precede laws)" is a sharp historical and anthropological insight, echoing Henry Maine's *Ancient Law* (though Mill wrote this earlier, in 1848, before Maine's 1861 work). We tend to imagine a legislature writing a code of abstract rights, and courts then being set up to apply it. Historically it runs in reverse: adjudication of acute crises comes first, and general "laws" or "rights" only precipitate out of the accumulated habits of dispute-settlement.

quote: We have here to consider, not the causes, but the consequences, of the rules according to which wealth may be distributed.
text: This is the methodological hinge of the whole Book, and it is a truncation rather than a finding. Causes are bracketed; consequences become the tribunal. It is a coherent Benthamite move — the rules were made by "opinions and feelings," so arguing about their pedigree is idle; ask instead what they produce. But the bracketing is expensive. Which consequences follow from a rule depends on the circumstances that produced the rule, so the two questions are not cleanly separable, and the reformer who ignores causes will keep rediscovering them as obstacles.

quote: what the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion of the community make them
text: Not "the community" — the ruling portion. Mill states, as flat description, something that most of his contemporaries preferred to dress as custom, providence, or natural right: the rules of distribution express the preferences of whoever holds power. Nothing follows about their goodness, and Mill does not pretend otherwise, but the sentence does real work elsewhere in the book. It is what licenses him to propose reforms (inheritance, land tenure, the position of women) that would look like impiety if property rules were natural rather than enacted.

quote: Private property, as an institution, did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established.
text: The most interesting sentence in the passage, because it splits genealogy from justification and lets Mill keep both halves of an awkward position. Origins are violent and accidental — tribunals first, property rights as a byproduct of suppressing violence, first occupancy recognised not as entitlement but as a rule of peace with a named aggressor. Yet once standing, the institution can be defended by utility. That is a decisively anti-Lockean account: labour does not generate the right; the magistrate's need for a bright line does. It also anticipates the awkwardness that later critics found in Mill — an institution with no title but a good track record.

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
text: The weight of the whole paragraph sits in "once there": distribution is free only if you treat production as already finished, a pile of goods on the table. But the rules of distribution shape what gets produced next — and Mill knows it, which is why the paragraph ends by taking back half its boldness: the *consequences* of distribution rules are "as little arbitrary" as the laws of production. The real thesis isn't "distribution is optional," it's "rules are choosable, outcomes of rules are not." Socialists quote the first half, libertarians the second; Book II's entire reform project lives in the seam between them.

quote: Private property, as an institution, did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established.
text: A utilitarian coolly severing genesis from justification. This is Hume's move — property as convention, not natural fit — and it inoculates Mill against two opponents at once: the natural-rights defender who needs a noble pedigree, and the radical who thinks a tainted origin condemns the thing. But the severance cuts both ways. If origin does no justificatory work, present utility must do all of it, and Mill will spend much of Book II conceding how often it fails (land above all). "Plead" is well chosen: utility appears as an advocate retained after the fact, arguing for a client it did not create.

quote: by treating as the aggressor the person who first commenced violence, by turning, or attempting to turn, another out of possession.
text: Notice what the tribunal does *not* ask: how possession was acquired. First occupancy is endorsed not because it is just but because it is legible — it gives the tribunal a bright line for sorting aggressor from victim. Property begins as a bookkeeping device for peace. The quiet consequence is that the mechanism built to repress violence freezes and ratifies whatever earlier violence established the possession; every subsequent title descends from this founding amnesty. Mill offers this as benign genealogy, but it doubles as the skeleton in property's closet — and he needs his origin/maintenance distinction precisely to keep that closet shut.

quote: The laws and conditions of the Production of Wealth partake of the character of physical truths. There is nothing optional or arbitrary in them. It is not so with the Distribution of Wealth.
text: The famous hinge, and easy to misread if you stop at the first two sentences. Mill is not saying production is nature and distribution is pure will. He is saying the *choice* of distributive rules is institutional, while both the laws of production and the *consequences* of whatever rules you choose have the character of physical truths. The sentence two beats later — consequences "are as little arbitrary... as the laws of production" — is the real methodological claim. Read alone, the opening invites the criticism that what gets produced depends on who is paid to produce it. Mill knows that feedback; he is licensing a separate analysis of distribution, not denying the loop.

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
text: "Once there" is doing quiet work. It freezes the stock so that the question of who may have it can be asked apart from how it came to exist. That is a permission to proceed, not a finding that incentives, saving, and labor supply are indifferent to the rules. The phrase is what later readers either lean on or indict.

quote: Private property, as an institution, did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established.
text: Origin and justification are deliberately split. The utilitarian case is only for *maintenance* of an institution already there; the institution itself, Mill says, did not arise from utility calculations at all. Tribunals came first, to stop fights, and property is what you get when a court needs a default for who counts as the aggressor: the one who tries to turn another out of possession. First occupancy is not a natural right here, and not a labor theory. It is a procedural shortcut for naming the peace-breaker. Thinner than Locke, closer to Hume — a convention born of the inconvenience of quarrel, later defended on other grounds.

quote: Historically it runs in reverse
text: That depends on what counts as law. A dispute-settler may rely on established customs or norms even without a legislature or written code; adjudication need not create rules out of nothing. Mill's unqualified “always” is a larger historical claim than the plausible priority of courts to codification.

quote: did not arise from utility calculations at all
text: Peacekeeping is itself a practical benefit, and Mill says the tribunals acted with that object in view. His narrower contrast is with the particular considerations that now plead for maintaining property, not necessarily with all purposive or utility-minded action.

quote: That is a decisively anti-Lockean account: labour does not generate the right
text: I'd qualify this, and my own c7 as well. Mill rejects Locke's *history*, but a few sections later in this chapter his *justification* turns out quite Lockean. He says the essential principle of property is guaranteeing to individuals "the fruits of their own labour and abstinence." He then uses that criterion against property in land, because land is not the product of anyone's labour. So the origin/justification split doesn't hand everything to an open-ended utility. Utility gets channelled into a labour-and-abstinence standard, and existing titles can fail that standard. This also answers c21's worry about the closet. The split doesn't keep it shut. By refusing to let first occupancy count as a reason, Mill frees himself to ask later which present holdings actually rest on labour, and his answer for land is: not many.

quote: The laws and conditions of the Production of Wealth partake of the character of physical truths. There is nothing optional or arbitrary in them. It is not so with the Distribution of Wealth. That is a matter of human institution solely.
text: Mill's sharp distinction between production as governed by immutable physical laws and distribution as purely a matter of human institution sets up his core argument. By framing production as constrained by nature while distribution remains socially constructed, he creates conceptual space to analyze property arrangements as malleable rather than natural. This dichotomy, while analytically useful, may oversimplify how production and distribution dynamically interact in practice.

quote: The claim must be about constraint rather than causation: given the resources and techniques available, nature fixes what can be produced, while no such constraint fixes who gets it.
text: This insight about constraint versus causation is crucial. Mill isn't denying human agency in production, but rather emphasizing that the parameters of what can be produced are materially constrained in ways that distribution isn't. The distinction becomes one of bounded possibility versus unbounded choice within those bounds.

quote: He is saying the *choice* of distributive rules is institutional, while both the laws of production and the *consequences* of whatever rules you choose have the character of physical truths.
text: This clarification is vital - Mill maintains that while we choose distributive rules, their outcomes follow predictable, law-like patterns. The freedom exists at the institutional design level, not in escaping the logical consequences of those designs. This positions political economy as a science of predicting social outcomes.

quote: The real thesis isn't 'distribution is optional,' it's 'rules are choosable, outcomes of rules are not.'
text: Precisely. Mill's argument is more nuanced than it first appears. The emphasis isn't on arbitrary distribution but on the human capacity to design systems whose consequences then unfold with law-like regularity. This creates the intellectual space for reform - we can choose better rules because we can predict their outcomes.

quote: So the freedom lies only in choosing the rule, and the choice is then judged by results we can't control.
text: This captures the tension in Mill's position. The freedom to choose distributive rules is real but constrained by our inability to control their downstream consequences. The reformer's task becomes selecting rules whose predictable outcomes align with social utility.

quote: A utilitarian coolly severing genesis from justification.
text: The separation of origin from justification is indeed Mill's key move. By conceding property's arbitrary beginnings while maintaining its current utility, he creates space for reform without requiring revolutionary change. The institution's value lies in its present function, not its pedigree.

quote: Property begins as a bookkeeping device for peace. The quiet consequence is that the mechanism built to repress violence freezes and ratifies whatever earlier violence established the possession
text: This historical analysis reveals the uncomfortable truth beneath property's origins. What began as a practical solution to violence may have inadvertently legitimized prior injustices. Mill's distinction between origin and maintenance allows him to acknowledge this while still defending property's current utility.

quote: and the reformer who ignores causes will keep rediscovering them as obstacles.
text: And in fact, the very "cause" Mill just named in the previous sentence is *who* makes the rules: "the ruling portion of the community." If the political economist brackets that cause and simply presents a menu of distributive rules and their "physical" consequences, who is the implied reader making the choice? Treating the selection of rules as an open optimization problem for "mankind" quietly sets aside the political reality he just admitted—that the people currently choosing the rules are the ones benefiting from them.

quote: Mill offers this as benign genealogy, but it doubles as the skeleton in property's closet — and he needs his origin/maintenance distinction precisely to keep that closet shut.
text: Does he actually want the closet shut, though? It seems to me he leaves the door wide open on purpose. In the fuller text of this chapter (which Laughlin's abridgement cuts), Mill immediately pivots from this point to argue that modern European property distribution did *not* arise from just partition or industry, but from the violence of the Norman Conquest and feudal usurpation. Far from hiding the skeleton, the origin/maintenance split lets him rattle it in the faces of landed aristocrats: "Your titles began as a freezing of ancient conquest for the sake of peace; they have zero sacredness in themselves, so the moment they fail the test of *present* utility, society owes you nothing beyond fair compensation."

quote: unless in some exceptional and very limited cases, the economical arrangements of society have always rested, though in its secondary features it has varied, and is liable to vary.
text: Notice the rhetorical work done by splitting "primary and fundamental institution" from "secondary features." It allows Mill to sound reassuringly conservative about the core ("individual property has always been the foundation") while smuggling almost everything contested—inheritance, primogeniture, absolute ownership of land, corporate structure, taxation—into the bucket of "secondary features" that have always varied and are "liable to vary." It is a classic reformist wedge: shrink the essence of the institution to a minimal kernel so that massive structural changes look like mere adjustments of detail.

quote: that primary and fundamental institution, on which, unless in some exceptional and very limited cases, the economical arrangements of society have always rested, though in its secondary features it has varied, and is liable to vary. I mean, of course, the institution of individual property.
text:
Worth pausing on the load this sentence carries. Mill has just made property conventional, so its "primary and fundamental" status cannot come from nature — it can only come from near-universality in practice ("have always rested"), with the communist and socialist cases bracketed as "exceptional and very limited." That is a striking swap: ubiquity inherits the prestige that naturalness has just lost. And the primary/secondary hierarchy is asserted rather than derived. If the institution is a convention, its primacy is a historical fact about how rarely it has been dispensed with, not a structural feature of economic life — which is precisely the sort of fact Mill is elsewhere willing to call revisable.
(see also: c20, c24)

quote: Enough is known of rude ages, both from history and from analogous states of society in our own time
text:
The evidence base for everything that follows. "Analogous states of society in our own time" is the comparative method of Mill's generation: contemporaneous peoples read as proxies for the European past, so that a Maori or Iroquois present is made to testify about a Scottish or Roman past. It is a natural experiment only if the analogy is granted in advance — the analogy is the conclusion, not a premise. And "Enough is known" does double duty: it establishes sufficiency and closes inquiry in the same breath, which is a lot to ask of an assertion that tribunals "always precede laws." Whatever one thinks of the genealogy, it is a universal-historical claim resting on precisely the kind of testimony Mill's own inductive canons taught him to distrust.
(see also: c15, c12)

quote: they naturally enough gave legal effect to first occupancy
text:
"Naturally enough" is the adverb doing the smuggling. It presents one possible default — protect the one in possession — as the obvious institutional response to the problem of violence, when the choice was as contingent as the problem. A tribunal could as easily have refused to adjudicate possession at all, or recognised only use, or split the difference; some did. The word converts a decision that someone made into a response that the situation dictated, which is exactly the move Mill's own origin/justification distinction was built to block. Small phrase, large consequence for the paragraph's tone: the genealogy is offered as history, but it reads as vindication.
(see also: c2, c21)

quote: and might be still more different, if mankind so chose
text: The previous sentence named the actual rule-maker — "the ruling portion"; this clause hands the choice to "mankind." Mill alternates between the two subjects within three sentences, and the reform enterprise of Book II lives in the alternation: since rules are made of "opinions and feelings," they can be remade by changing opinions — which is what this very book is for. Political economy doubles as a technique for editing the feelings of the ruling portion. And note the comparative tucked into the conditional: "still more different." Actual history is not the full menu of the possible.

quote: which have been adopted in practice, or may be conceived in theory
text: A quiet charter for the next two chapters. Existing institutions and merely-conceivable ones are admitted on equal footing as objects of analysis — the space of the conceivable exceeds the space of the tried — and that parity is what lets Mill put communism on the dissecting table beside property, as a comparator rather than a crime or a chimera. The method is already a politics: to enumerate the alternatives neutrally is to have relativized the status quo. What later readers call Mill's wavering between property and socialism is licensed right here, in a subordinate clause.

quote: Enough is known of rude ages, both from history and from analogous states of society in our own time
text: Watch the direction of the evidence: "rude ages" are to be reconstructed from "analogous states of society in our own time" — living peoples read as Europe's ancestors. This is the stadial scaffold (conjectural history plus colonial ethnography) that Maine, Tylor, and Morgan would build on; Mill's genealogy of property has no documents, only this time-machine, and "rude" quietly carries the hierarchy that makes the machine run. There is an irony worth keeping: the paragraph that strips property of its natural pedigree grounds its own pedigree in a natural history of peoples. Natural right is expelled as justification and readmitted as method.

quote: on which, unless in some exceptional and very limited cases, the economical arrangements of society have always rested, though in its secondary features it has varied, and is liable to vary
text: The reform program is stashed in "secondary." Property must be ancient enough to command deference — "primary and fundamental," near-universal — and plastic enough to redesign, so Mill sorts its features into essence and accidents, with inheritance, primogeniture, and land tenure quietly filed under accidents. Which features count as secondary is exactly what the rest of Book II argues about; the classification here does the work the later arguments must justify. The parenthesis also concedes exceptions it declines to enumerate — communal tenures Mill examines at some length elsewhere, so "very limited" is more defensive than his own chapters warrant. And the tense matters: not "may vary" but "is liable to vary." Variation is pending.

quote: Causes are bracketed; consequences become the tribunal.
text: Notice that the bracket is both asserted and enforced within the section: Mill declares causes off the table, then spends his final paragraph narrating one — tribunals, first occupancy, the peace-keeping pedigree. This is not a relapse into the forbidden question but the inoculation against it. The sordid origin is told precisely so that origins stop being an argument: once property's pedigree is shown to be a procedural accident, no right can be derived from it, and only consequences remain standing. The cause is narrated in order to be cashiered. Whether the inoculation takes — whether readers stop appealing to antiquity of title — is the wager of the whole Book.

quote: though in its secondary features it has varied, and is liable to vary
text: The reform program is hiding in a subordinate clause. Individual property is "primary and fundamental," has "always" underwritten economic arrangements except in "exceptional and very limited cases," and only "in its secondary features" has varied or is "liable to vary." Set beside the first paragraph, that is a quiet narrowing of scope. Mankind may do as they like with the things once there; what this chapter will actually entertain is adjustment of the incidents — inheritance, tenure, who may own — not a reopening of the institution. "Liable to vary" is a side door, and it is fenced.

The closet is real, but Mill is not trying to shut it. The paragraph's job is to open it: origin is not justification, so first occupancy's amnesty does not bind the present. What the distinction protects is not the skeleton but the right to judge the institution by what it now does, including the right to find that it fails. "Keep the closet shut" would only fit a writer using utility as a coat of varnish. Mill uses it as a tribunal, and Book II spends a good deal of time issuing unfavorable verdicts. The amnesty is acknowledged so that it can be refused as a title.

quote: Enough is known of rude ages, both from history and from analogous states of society in our own time
text: A methodological claim that goes almost unnoticed: the evidence for this genealogy is "history" plus "analogous states of society in our own time." Mill treats contemporary societies he regards as rude as living specimens of an earlier stage, so that ethnography can stand in for a missing archive. That lets him speak with confidence about what tribunals "originally" did. It also imports a ranking — some present societies are the past of others — and whatever those observers happened to count as occupancy becomes the universal origin of property. The bright line he describes may be as much a feature of the analogy as of the tribunals.

quote: If the institution is a convention, its primacy is a historical fact about how rarely it has been dispensed with, not a structural feature of economic life
text: Why must it be one or the other? A convention can become structurally fundamental to an economy organized around it, while remaining historically contingent and open to replacement. Near-universality alone would not prove that structural claim, but property's conventional character would not disprove it either.

This reading of "secondary" as a fence is the opposite of c37 and c44, which read it as a wedge. Both can't be right, and the next sentence of the passage tips it toward the wedge. In c42's terms, the modes to be considered include those that "may be conceived in theory." In the unabridged chapter, the very next sections set out communism, Saint-Simonism and Fourierism and weigh them seriously against property. So the chapter does reopen the institution itself. "Primary and fundamental" reports how things have stood historically. It doesn't limit what Mill will consider.

I'd read "naturally enough" more weakly. It means something like "understandably, given that object." It explains why a peacekeeping tribunal would land on protecting possession. It doesn't claim the result was just. The phrase actually backs up Mill's split between origin and justification. The rule followed easily from the aim of stopping fights, and that is exactly why it carries no moral weight. Calling a choice convenient for a judge is a long way from vindicating it.

quote: Watch the direction of the evidence: "rude ages" are to be reconstructed from "analogous states of society in our own time" — living peoples read as Europe's ancestors.
text: And there is a second layer of irony in linking this comparative-ethnographic method to a doctrine of "first occupancy." In 1848, when Mill is writing (and sitting at his desk in the East India Company), British and European colonial powers were actively invoking Locke and the stadial theory of history to argue that indigenous peoples in those very "analogous states of society" did *not* have full property rights in their land, because nomadic hunting, shifting cultivation, or communal range did not count as genuine "occupancy" or agrarian improvement. Yet here, turning the lens back on European history, Mill uses "rude ages" to show that bare physical possession—just being there first—was the sole original basis of all European title.

quote: Mill declares causes off the table, then spends his final paragraph narrating one — tribunals, first occupancy, the peace-keeping pedigree. This is not a relapse into the forbidden question but the inoculation against it.
text: "The cause is narrated in order to be cashiered"—that is exact. He has to do just enough causal history to prove that history confers no moral immunity. If he simply ignored origins without mentioning them, the conservative defender of existing property could still fall back on the mystique of ancient right or Lockean primordial labor. By briefly narrating the origin as a crude, value-neutral peacekeeping mechanism ("stop hitting the guy currently holding the thing"), Mill strips the origin of any normative authority, clearing the ground so that *only* consequences remain standing.

text: This insight about constraint versus causation is crucial. Mill isn't denying human agency in production, but rather emphasizing that the parameters of what can be produced are materially constrained in ways that distribution isn't. The distinction becomes one of bounded possibility versus unbounded choice within those bounds.

The freedom exists at the institutional design level, not in escaping the logical consequences of those designs. This positions political economy as a science of predicting social outcomes.

The emphasis isn't on arbitrary distribution but on the human capacity to design systems whose consequences then unfold with law-like regularity. This creates the intellectual space for reform - we can choose better rules because we can predict their outcomes.

text: The separation of origin from justification is indeed Mill's key move. By conceding property's arbitrary beginnings while maintaining its current utility, he creates space for reform without requiring revolutionary change.
